Cavity magnomechanics provides a unique setting for exploring the macroscopic quantum effects by merging magnons, phonons, and photons into a singular system.  By integrating a two-dimensional magnetic material in one of the cavity mirrors, researchers have now proposed an innovative system for magnomechanics with nonlinear phonon-magnon interactions, something not previously achievable with traditional yttrium iron garnet based systems.  The newly designed setup yields an incredibly strong interaction between magnons and phonons, leading to the observation of a purely mechanical quantum effect - zero-point motion induced phonon absorption.  The resulting phenomenon of magnomechanics could soon enable the development of ultra-sensitive magnetic sensors.  The design of the setup also presents an excellent opportunity for studying the characteristics of magnons in two-dimensional magnetic materials, through the observation of magnon-phonon interactions using advanced thermophysics methods.  The integration of magnons, phonons, and photons in this system provides a comprehensive platform for exploring the principles of quantum physics, ultimately contributing to the advancement of quantum technology and fundamental research. \textit{See also: }C. The relation between a galaxy's mass in stars and its surrounding dark matter halo mass has been established for early-type galaxies by analyzing their near-infrared brightness and globular cluster distributions. By employing a dynamic model and applying a cosmological constraint, the mass of each halo was calculated, resulting in a star-to-halo mass relation with varying rates for different galaxy masses. It was found that early-type galaxies experience a decrease in mass relation after reaching their peak, which occurs around a mass ten times that of our sun. This result agrees with previously obtained constraints from weak lensing data. Furthermore, the late-type galaxies in the sample were discovered to have lower stellar masses than early-type galaxies of the same brightness, which indicates that they require more massive halos to explain their emission. It was also found that the early-type galaxies in the sample are surrounded by smaller halos than would be expected if they were part of galaxy groups or clusters, which indicates that many of them may be isolated or in less dense environments. Finally, the calculation of the fraction of a galaxy's mass in stars, when compared to its surrounding halo, resulted in a bell-shaped distribution over a wide range of masses, which indicates that the process of star formation does not simply cease early in the galaxy's development but, rather, varies according to a galaxy's mass. This could make it difficult for galaxies with lower masses to form supermassive black holes through the Eddyprocess, which is necessary for their initial development. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and conducted experiments to improve this technique. Through these experiments, we were able to achieve a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth using paired green and yellow photometry. This advancement enabled us to detect tiny changes in the aerosol depth as large as 0.003 within a single hour, comparable to detecting a daily temperature change of 0.1 K. This new precision is equivalent to being able to tell the difference between one grain of rice at a distance of 1 kilometer. This improved technique is expected to be useful for monitoring the atmosphere during future astrophysics research at the telescope and will also support other research at the Pierre Auger Observatory by increasing the detectability of local aerosol changes during satellite transits and enhancing the accuracy of particle density measurements by comparing paired photometry with optical depth measurements. This new technique is openly available through an interactive web page that allows users to explore the data and code. The website is at https://stella.auger.edu/. Our team is committed to continuing to enhance this technique and welcomes suggestions and contributions from the community to help achieve a precision of 0.001 for measuring the aerosol depth, a precision that would allow us to monitor the atmosphere as accurately as weather forecasting. To accomplish this goal, we plan to use machine learning techniques to analyze data from future astrophysics research at the telescope and to make efficient use of computing resources by developing scalable code for comparing paired photometry with optical depth measurements. We generated theoretical forecasts for the cm-wavelength free-free emission produced by two distinct disk models, tailored to the TW Hydrae young stellar object, and analyzed how photoevaporation affects this phenomenon. According to our analysis, the high-energy photons from the star in systems like TW Hydrae can drive disk photoevaporation and create inner hole diameters of approximately 0.7 times the Hill radius. In contrast, our model reveals that the photoevaporation process produces a distinctive emission profile with a sharp decrease in intensity towards lower velocities, which can be attributed to the disk's wind and creates a dual-component structure separated by about 100-150 km/s. Furthermore, our results indicate that the radio continuum emission produced by free-free processes in systems like TW Hydrae is primarily influenced by the disk's inner region and outer wind component rather than the disk's bulk. We also compared our theoretical forecasts to actual observational data from TW Hydrae, finding general agreement with data at velocities below 100 km/s but observing some discrepancies, such as a lack of our model's predicted intensity in higher velocity ranges. Nevertheless, our analysis highlights the need for data that can accurately quantify the mass loss rate and inner hole diameter in systems like TW Hydrae. In the future, our model foresees the potential for radio interferometry to shed more light on this phenomenon by generating high-resolution images of the system and quantifying its dynamical and morphological characteristics. In particular, our study predicts that the inner hole diameter can be estimated by examining the velocity-gradients of the emission profile, which is sensitive to this diameter, at velocities above 100 km/s. We also speculate that the X-shape emission profile observed in systems like TW Hydrae could be attributed to the presence of a disk gap created by a planet or a massive dust grain storm, which restricts the radial diffusion of the gas. In the future, our study aspires to explore the potential for our model to detect the signature of a planet or dust grains storm in systems like TW Hydrae by creating artificial images of the system and analyzing the difference between various models. In particular, our study predicts that the inner orbit of a planet or dust grains storm would produce a distinctive drop in intensity towards lower velocities in the emission profile, which would create a 'U-shape' rather than 'M-shape' component, and would also modify the wind's emission profile such that the 'M-shape' component would appear shifted towards higher velocities, creating a second 'M-shape' component beyond the Hill radius

For speech processing applications, tasks such as speech voicing, fundamental frequency estimation, and dynamic pitch tracking are essential components that require efficient algorithms to accomplish. To meet this need, we have developed a novel algorithm that integrates these subtasks into a single unified procedure, allowing it to effectively handle pre-recorded speech with significant background noise levels. The algorithm utilizes a set of established metrics, like the zero-crossing rate, to create an unsupervised voicing classification system, and a hybrid approach based on autocorrelation is used to calculate pitch values. To improve the accuracy of pitch tracking, we have implemented a forward-backward algorithm inspired by the Kalman filter. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing pitch detection and tracking techniques, particularly in environments with high background noise levels. The proposed algorithm has been successfully applied in a pre-recorded speech analysis system, where it has shown efficacy in facilitating rapid and accurate location of speech segments within the audio data. The role of neural architecture search (NAS) has escalated within the deep learning community in recent years, however its full potential is constrained by most current approaches when dealing with complex and vast search spaces. Our proposal tackles this issue by incorporating NAS within a broader framework of efficient machine learning program search, allowing for the discovery of intricate architectures within a more comprehensive search space. Our approach exploits relationships between neural architectures and their functional properties to reduce the program search space, thereby making NAS possible on more efficient and accurate estimators. By searching for a once-dominant architecture within the Program Search space, our method demonstrates superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art NAS methods on standard benchmarks, while also revealing the previously overlooked potential in Program Search. The advantages and limitations of multicast beamforming for millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems using massive arrays. By combining semidefinite relaxation and deep learning-based methods, we optimize non-orthogonal precoders that balance multicasting performance and user decorrelation. The proposed hybrid design is evaluated in a simulated urban environment and shows significant improvements in multicast throughput, user correlation, and spectrum efficiency compared to conventional methods. Experimental results reveal that a substantial portion of mmWave bandwidth can be allocated for multicasting before significantly decreasing due to increased user correlation, offering a useful threshold for multicasting in practice. Moreover, our findings suggest that multibeam precoders with a moderate number of beams can yield satisfactory performance, reducing complex computations associated with larger systems. These findings advocate for the integration of multicasting in mmWave systems using massive arrays. The proposed approach can also serve as a foundation for designingunicast hybrid precoders that balance spectral efficiency and user correlation. The simulated performance gains of our design over conventional methods lie in the range of 10-40%, depending on the system configuration. The remaining challenges and open problems for optimizing hybrid precoders are addressed in the context of rapidly evolving 5G and 6G wireless networks. Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. A new Federated Learning paradigm, Federated Distillation, has been developed with distinct communication properties. It employs ensemble distillation and transfers model outputs as soft labels to participating clients and a central server via a public data set. Unlike conventional Federated Learning, such as Federated Averaging, which increases communication complexity with model size, Federated Distillation reduces communication complexity by utilizing the size of the distillation data set. We analyzed the potential for communication efficiency in Federated Distillation by evaluating the effects of curation techniques, soft-label quantization, and delta-coding. The results guided the development of Compressed Federated Distillation, a highly efficient method for Federated Distillation. Experiments on image classification and language modeling showcased the potential for significant communication savings, achieving reductions of more than two orders of magnitude over Federated Distillation and four orders of magnitude over Federated Averaging, while maintaining fixed performance levels. The mathematical framework of Federated Distillation was also formalized and found to be equivalent to minimizing a Kullback-Liebler divergence, offering insights into its convergence properties. The code for Compressed Federated Distillation can be found at https://github.com/alexalexar/compressed-federated-distillation. A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support future-proof services on large networks of interconnected computers. Our study examines how to effectively manage the flow of service requests across an NDN-based network, considering the varying capabilities of each node to process and generate data. Focusing on service workflows with connected components, we develop an algorithm for online, distributed control of each node's decision-making processes. Our proposed Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO) method aims to achieve lower overall delays and optimal data transmission rates. It combines queuing strategies and routing discipline based on topology, using network information acquired through a new discovery approach, allowing for efficient performance under uncertain conditions. We validate SDADO with analytical models and numerical simulations demonstrating reduced end-to-end delays and optimal data transmission rates. Notably, SDADO offers adjustable delay sensitivity, allowing users to balance this factor with actual speeds. We also explore an optimization problem to find the optimal delay target, given a pre-determined level of transmission quality. Numerical investigations of this issue are conducted, and evidence showing the effectiveness of SDADO is compiled from simulation results. All the mentioned concepts and algorithms are implemented in an open-source simulator to verify their functionality. It is expected that the proposed methods will contribute to the development of more efficient service distribution mechanisms in NDN-based networks. We tackle the exponential stability of a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam situated on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. These branches are denoted as $I_j$, for $j = 1, 2, 3$. The point where the branches meet is called $\Delta$, and the distance from $\Delta$ to the origin is parameterized as $b > 0$. The interior point $x_i$ is fixed on each branch. The main aim here is to investigate how the located interior point affects the stability of the system, particularly how it influences the eigenvectors and their exponential decay at the boundary $\partial I_j$. Some key findings include the boundedness of eigenvectors at $\partial I_j$, their behavior near $\Delta$, and a specific representation related to the vertex $\Delta$. The fourth eigenfunction exhibits distinct behavior and can be analyzed separately. Furthermore, the decay rates of certain eigenfunctions are tied to the first zero of the corresponding Euler-Bernoulli eigenfunctions on a simple interval. To confirm exponential stability, we demonstrate the existence of a suitable Lyapunov function and derive its properties, including its boundary behavior and its relation to the graph's vertices. In addition, certain $L^2$-norms of specific elliptic equations on $I_j$ are connected to the decay rates of eigenvectors at $\partial I_j$. These connections allow us to easily determine the located interior point's effect on the system's stability. Specifically, if the interior point is located at a boundary, the system becomes unstable. Conversely, if the interior point is far from the boundary, the system remains stable, and the decay rates can be calculated using modified versions of Del Ronde's inequality. To confirm these claims, we construct a suitable Lyapunov function and derive its properties, including its boundary behavior and its relation to the graph's vertices. Some key findings include the system's independence of $p$ and $\mu$ and the system's decay rates being influenced by the located interior point and the connected elliptic equations on $I_j$. Ultimately, the system's exponential stability is confirmed, and the decay rates can be calculated using the provided formulas. To illustrate these claims, several numerical examples are included. Utilizing ternary chemical potential phase diagrams and phonon spectrum analysis,
our research shows that compounds $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ ($M$ = Cd, Hg), derived from Tl$_5$Te$_3$,
exhibit stability in their body-centered tetragonal crystal structure with symmetry $I$4/$mcm$.
Our calculations also indicate the occurrence of a significant band inversion in $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$
at the Fermi level and the generation of a 0.13 eV topological band gap in CdTl$_4$Te$_3$
due to the influence of spin-orbit coupling. The predicted topological insulating properties
make $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ candidates for efficient 3D strong topological insulator research and the
potential utilization of extrinsic surface control through chemical doping. Additionally, our
study reveals that $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ exhibits an unusual anisotropic charge carrier behavior with
an exceptionally high $n$/$p$ ratio, further confirming the materials' suitability for the study
of unusual transport phenomena. Our calculations are validated by X-ray diffraction and
transport measurements conducted on CdTl$_4$Te$_3$. As an added aspect, our findings from
naive transport suggest the presence of unconventional quantum Hall effects in this
material. Preliminary transport analysis demonstrates the presence of these effects, and
detailed quantum transport studies are required to confirm this hypothesis. Instead of
conclusively determining the Hall effect, our research primarily highlights the potential of
$M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ as a platform for this research. Experimental verification of these phenomena
is anticipated to facilitate innovative developments using $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ as a versatile material
platform for in-depth research of exotic phenomena.

The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through interactive learning or machine learning algorithms. However, these methods have their own shortcomings - the first assumes a perfectly defined utility function, interactive learning can be time-consuming and laborious, and machine learning algorithms often make unwarranted assumptions about the problem structure. In contrast, this paper proposes a novel method where experts directly define the desired trade-offs between objectives, utilizing conceptually simple and intuitive specialized utility functions. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a simulation of a cyber security problem, showing its capabilities to handle large problem dimensions and produce accurate results. Moreover, it's shown to outperform state-of-the-art multi-objective optimization methods in both a cyber security scenario and a modified version of the DTLZ test suite. In particular, when experts are involved, this method can achieve accuracy levels comparable to those of perfectly defined utility functions; and even without expert involvement, it performs competitively, especially in larger problem dimensions. The proposed method is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/neoagent/MOOCyber. Cyber security problems often pose significant challenges to optimization algorithms due to a large number of objectives and decision variables. In order to address this issue, a technique called knowledge-based mapping was used to simplify a particular cyber security problem, resulting in improved performance and accuracy. The integration of this technique with the proposed method confirmed its benefits and paved the way for the integration of knowledge-based constraints, which will be addressed in future work. The proposed method was successfully validated on a real-world non-linear aerodynamic optimization problem. Specifically, it was utilized to optimize the aerodynamic characteristics of a turbomachine in the OpenFOAM software, utilizing mesh morphing and gradient-based optimization. The results showed a significant improvement in aerodynamic performance, with a 42% increase in lift and a 56% decrease in drag, while maintaining stability through the application of stability functions. The proposed method offers several key benefits, including the ability to handle complex, high-dimensional problem spaces, and the ability to utilize expert knowledge to define desired trade-offs between objectives, resulting in accurate and efficient multi-objective optimization. Moreover, it is visible that the Pareto front is well-defined, with no discontinuities, and the desired balance between objectives is achieved. The proposed method is capable of handling at least 16 objectives and 10 decision variables, and can potentially handle more complex problem spaces in the future. Our investigation demonstrates that these vulnerabilities can be expanded from attacks that have knowledge of the agents and their training processes, to situations where no information is available. We employ sequence-to-sequence models to predict actions of trained agents based on sequence data. Our results reveal that these models effectively anticipate the future actions of RL agents across a broad range of scenarios, suggesting that these agents can be vulnerable in black-box environments. Moreover, while adversarial samples are transferable to RL agents, they demonstrate limited effectiveness compared to random noise, underscoring a flaw in previous assessments that relied solely on adversarial samples as a baseline. Furthermore, we propose a novel use for adversarial samples, which could be exploited by attackers to induce trained agents to malfunction after a specific time interval, opening up the potential for an 'agent-as-time-bomb' threat. In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) based on the entropic risk measure, we study an approach for solving non-stationary Markov decision processes (MDPs) in a fixed budget framework. The reward functions and state transitions are both unknown and change over time. With a known variation budget, we develop restart-based algorithms and derive their dynamic regret values. These findings serve as a basis for an adaptive algorithm without a prior variation budget requirement. The proposed method detects non-stationarity and yields a dynamic regret lower bound, demonstrating its near-optimality for risk-sensitive RL in changing environments. Moreover, our results demonstrate the feasibility of designing risk control and non-stationarity handling separately if the variation budget is known, and that adaptive detection of non-stationarity is possible without knowledge of the variation budget. The significance of our work lies in its relevance to practical situations such as navigating changing traffic patterns in self-driving cars. Businesses utilize issue tracking systems to keep tabs on their projects by dividing tasks into manageable issues. This documentation style fosters gradual improvement, as each issue can be reviewed, commented on, connected to related issues, and advanced through the company workflow. Well-studied platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bugzilla have received significant attention, whereas Jira, a highly-used tracking system with a wealth of accompanying information, remains underresearched. Due to difficulties in data collection, our analysis is confined to publicly accessible projects across nine domains, totaling 68 Jiras. Using automated tools to gather data on issue threads, our investigation offers insights into the evolution of these threads. This knowledge can be applied to develop predictive models for forecasting issue development. This knowledge can also be used to suggest possible applications of these models, such as assessing the likelihood of issues being resolved or closing on a timeline. By evaluating the performance of various machine learning algorithms, our results indicate that convolutional neural networks can effectively model issue development. This study is a initial step towards exploring the dynamics of issue tracking systems, and our hope is to stimulate further research on this topic, possibly expanding to more popular and widely-underresearched systems in the future. Our code, available at https://github.com/damienpr/ijcsm, serves as an entry point into our study for other researchers to build upon our findings. This code, along with our dataset, can be used to reproduce our results in addition to opening doors for novel applications of natural language models in the analysis of business workflow. Our analysis reveals that issue development can be accurately modeled using natural language models, striking a balance between simplicity and effectiveness. Our results suggest that QRCNN and 2D-GMM outperform other algorithms in forecasting issue closure, with a margin of 5%. Unlike prior research on software repositories, our investigation shows that vector-space based models can be applied to business workflow, outperforming topic modeling in forecasting issue closure. This study is the first to demonstrate the capability of deep learning algorithms in modeling business workflow, offering a versatile toolbox for forecasting various business metrics. Yet, standard DML approaches may not be well adapted to handle networks that shift in real time while operating on non-stationary data. In such scenarios, existing DML methods can lead to suboptimal models and slow convergence. In response, we propose a new framework, SPODL, that uses a model-based approach to adjust for network variations and non-stationary data. This approach ensures that learned models remain accurate and improve consistently. In addition, we also introduce average agreement based regularization to further enhance the framework's robustness and simplicity. In experiments using synthetic data and image classification, SPODL consistently outperformed other DML methods under various network conditions. In particular, SPODL showed improved model quality and lower training costs compared to the next best method. Moreover, we observed that SPODL's robustness came at a computational cost that was only slightly higher than other methods. In conclusion, the results validate SPODL as a reliable and efficient solution for distributed machine learning applications in time-varying networks. In future work, we plan to apply SPODL to real-world problems such as autonomous driving and image classification. In addition, we also intend to investigate the theoretical convergence properties of SPODL in detail. In particular, we aim to study how the learning rate and network changes affect the convergence of the model. This includes an optical dipole trap formed by the intersection of two laser beams of 850 nm, creating a pattern of traps with diameters of around 2.7 micrometers per atom, which guides a probe laser of 780 nm to stimulate and collect fluorescence emitted by the atoms. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, applications of the proposed approach have been successfully explored in the prediction of melting points in abiotic molecules. Additionally, a graphical user interface called POLYGEN has been developed to facilitate the utilization of the proposed approach by non-experts. This user-friendly tool allows users to input desired molecular properties, search for existing molecules, and even design new polymers with specific attributes. Notably, the accuracy of the predictive frameworks for abiotic molecules was enhanced to a precision of 0.75, surpassing the current state-of-art precision of 0.72 in the field. Experimental validation of the designed compounds using a small-scale laboratory experiment for melting point analysis was conducted, confirming the predicted properties of two compounds, namely the polymers derived from the monomer Alanine and the compound DGLA. This marks a groundbreaking achievement in the field, as the proposed approach is the first to accurately predict melting points in abiotic molecules using artificial neural networks. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our approach successfully obtained precise tidal volumes for both patients under various scenarios. Our contribution is dual-fold: we are introducing new applications of direct approach transcription theories to control problems with time-varying systems and estimating unknown system parameters; we are also adapting these theories to design counterfactual control policies that could potentially be used in other predictive maintenance and design problems in control theory. Our approach is expected to be used in future projects that involve the predictive maintenance and design for control-theoretic separation problems. A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism. Specifically, these groups can be classified into six distinct types, defined as specific groups of permutations. Additionally, we note that most of these groups cannot be expressed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of other types of rational maps. However, there are some exceptions, given by the actions of specific polynomials and a particular rational map with a unique characteristic function. This characteristic function, $f_0$, corresponds to a map with specific properties and a given name (Brunicki's map). Similarly, there is a correspondence between another set of these groups and the actions of specific quadratic rational maps, given by the iterations of certain quadratic polynomials. Furthermore, we also note that there are additional groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, given by specific quadratic compositions and a third degree composition, both of which have unique characteristic functions. These compositions are as follows: the first being the composition of $(z^2+1)$ and $(z^2+(z+1)^2)$, and the second being the composition of $(3z^2+1)$ and $(z^2+(3z+1)^2)$. Finally, it's also noted that there are infinite additional groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, given by specific rational maps with specific characteristics. These characteristic properties ensure that these groups are distinct from each other and all other groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, and that their definitions are uniquely defined by specific mathematical equations. The proof given for these claims uses specific mathematical techniques such as local properties and the properties of certain invariant fields, along with specific definitions and naming of certain characteristic functions, to justify the uniqueness and definition of these groups. The naming of these characteristic functions includes Brunicki's map, Horowitz's map, Horowitz's 2nd map, the Deligne-Rask map, and finally the Suzuki map. Utilizing the principles of $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing, we introduce an innovative method to isolate the physical properties of the hadronic higgs-like particles, $Y(4230)$ and $Y(4575)$, in the mixing process. Employing this method, we accurately determine the mixing matrix eigenvalues, weights, and mixing angles of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ system. Subsequently, we apply the formulae derived from this method to analyze the properties of the two particles, $Y(4230)$ and $Y(4575)$. By doing so, we find that the two particles cannot be confidently identified as the long-sought $\eta$ and $\eta'$, respectively. Nonetheless, our results do reveal that the $Y(4230)$ particle, featuring an approximate mass of $4230-4300$ MeV, possesses a substantial $\eta$ weight yet exhibits a notable $\eta'$ weight, thereby yielding a mixing angle of $\phi \sim -5^\circ$ to -$10^\circ$. Conversely, the $Y(4575)$ particle demonstrates a considerable $\eta$ weight in conjunction with a weight of the $\eta'$ resonance, thus yielding a mixing angle of $\phi \sim 10^\circ$ to $15^\circ$. Subsequently, we propose the possibility that the $Y(4230)$ particle might be identified as the long-sought $\eta$ particle and suggest a potential name change to the $\eta(4230)$ particle. This research introduces three indices for characterizing online signature templates based on distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability. 
Distinctiveness is evaluated through statistical analysis and a random signature assumption on a set of user signature examples.
Complexity is determined by examining the features of user signature examples.
Reliability, on the other hand, is estimated by assessing a validation set of user signature examples.
These three indices serve as indicators for measuring the performance of online verification systems against both random and intentional forgeries as well as the performance of genuine users providing valid signature examples.
Through experiments using different verification algorithms and three online signature datasets plus one keystroke dataset, the validity of these measures and their applications have been verified and demonstrated. 
Additionally, the study compares the properties of online signature templates with those of keystroke pressure templates. 
Ultimately, the paper presents options for enhancing the reliability of online verification systems by selecting distinctively characteristic user signature examples with lower complexity. 
This study's findings may also be applied to other biometric verification methods.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. Our primary objective is to promote sustainable NLP research addressing the complex needs of multilingual societies. This paper was completed as part of the IIIT 2020 Winter Research Meet project, supervised by Dr. Zuhair Mahmood.

Building on Griffiths' model of a quantum radiator, I expand upon it by developing theoretical models that represent heat generated by a particle over time and its interaction with the surrounding environment. These quantum radiation models imply a connection between a particle's past and future, raising the idea that a particle may need to have existed long enough to exhibit this temporal relationship. This phenomenon could serve as a physical evidence for the reality of quantum entanglement between a particle and its own past and future. Furthermore, I examine how this effect could be observed in real-world experiments, potentially using particles that have undergone high-energy collisions as probes. Notably, I find that while certain properties of this model may share similarities with the concept of holography, the temporal connection between a particle's past and future could provide a distinct test of holographic theories. Ultimately, I discuss the practical challenges and limitations of implementing these models to study quantum entanglement and their potential impact on our understanding of the universe. Additionally, I touch on the possibility that quantum radiation could serve as a means to encode information about the particle's past, offering an alternative to Hawking radiation as a source of information about the particle's existence. This encoded information could potentially allow us to determine the particle's age, offering a new and precise method for doing so. I develop this idea further in my book 'The Information paradox: Quantum radiation models and the particle's temporal relationship'. Measurements of charged-particle fragmentation in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at the LHC are carried out with the ATLAS detector. Fragmentation functions in proton-proton events with high-pT, isolated photons exhibit variations from those of inclusive jet events due to quark and gluon differences in fragmentation behavior. Fragmentation ratios of lead-lead events over proton-proton events are examined for jet quenching effects, depending on the color-charge of partons in the hot, high-energy medium. Peripheral lead-lead events display analogous fragmentation modifications in photon-tagged and inclusive jet events, yet central events reveal greater jet fragmentation modifications in the former. Calculations utilizing jet tomography predict such observations, suggesting that photons can serve as powerful probes of the LHC's high-energy environment. These findings intensify the need for more precise jet fragmentation measurements, ultimately aiming for 10% precision in lead-lead to proton-proton ratios to firmly establish the evolution of partons in the LHC's high-energy medium. Until then, further exploration of photon-tagged and inclusive jet data will continue to provide crucial insights into the nature of jet quenching in nuclear collisions. This theoretical work offers a comprehensive framework for evaluating the accuracy of proposed methods in pose estimation tasks. Initially, we introduce a generalised approach for predicting pose estimation metrics, which can be applied to a wide range of problems (e.g. object, light or camera localization). By utilising observed data and a suitable representation of the target, we derive an expression for the expected error metric, which is subsequently used to calculate the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound. This lower bound serves as a baseline to assess existing methods and evaluate their performance. We also explore the benefits of using optimal parameterization to achieve precision close to theoretical limits. In addition, a novel and efficient gradient-based method is developed for high-speed optimization, which minimises deviations from the ideal solution. In order to validate our framework, we tested it on recently published state-of-the-art papers and observed a significant discrepancy between the predicted errors in simulated scenarios and the actual outcomes. We attributed these discrepancies to suboptimal initialization techniques and suggested various strategies for enhancing performance. Ultimately, we provide a unified software framework that integrates these techniques and can be used as a benchmark for evaluating future methods. This open-source package can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/constantinwimmer/pose estimation. For reproducibility purposes, we also include a step-by-step guide to creating similar visualisation tools and reproducing the presented results. Additionally, we share a video illustrating the proposed framework: https://youtu.be/px2hKTPKOIk. Based on our evaluation, we contend that an accurate assessment of pose estimation methods requires thorough experimentation guided by a solid theoretical foundation. We also argue that our framework has the potential to inspire novel methods which can surpass current benchmarks and achieve precision close to theoretical limits. At the time of writing, the proposed framework demonstrated a notable shortfall in performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of computational efficiency. Nonetheless, we are confident that future advancements in this domain will bridge this gap and lead to the development of even more effective algorithms. The advent of online collaboration tools like GitHub has made it easy for software developers to share and reuse code, even across project boundaries.  This research investigates how software maintenance professionals share and benefit from code snippets, which are often extracted from various tooling projects during the development process.  A code library called SMAP, which utilizes a graph database to store code snippets and their interconnected tools, has been developed to support this study.  By integrating a visualizer, researchers can navigate the code library and gain a deeper understanding of the code reuse patterns within it.  Empirical studies were conducted to identify common code reuse patterns and shareable tooling maintenance knowledge.  Results show that there is a high demand for maintaining existing tooling projects, even when new tools are introduced.  This finding highlights the importance of "meta-maintenance" - the practice of reusing existing tooling projects - and suggests that existing tooling projects can be effectively reused in new projects when provided with effective documentation and support.  By addressing the limitations of current methodological approaches, this research provides a foundation for exploring the concept of meta-maintenance and promotes further investigation into code reuse patterns and shared tooling maintenance knowledge. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Loss Minimization (MDLM) strategy to minimize the predicted rating differences between each domain and a unified general domain. By matching the domain-specific preferences of a target user to the actual ratings provided by another user in the general domain, MDLM promotes more accurate predictions in each domain. Through comprehensive evaluation of our proposed framework on four real-world datasets, MSDCR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR methods in terms of AUC@k, showcasing its superiority without relying on a well-supplied domain. The source code is available at https://github.com/ArgKuo/MSDCR.

To investigate the transportation and yield production of the $J/\psi$ in 200-GeV gold-gold collisions, a kinetic-rate equation is employed, taking into account the influence of shadowing and absorption while utilizing measured cross-sections from proton-proton interactions as well as equilibrium limits derived from thermal models. Specifically, we examine the effects of transport parameters such as the average equilibrium limit and average scattering probability in non-equilibrium conditions on $J/\psi$ behavior. These transport parameters are evaluated based on the $J/\psi$ mass and the characteristics of parton-parton cross-sections, with the outcome indicating that the $J/\psi$ is largely influenced by direct parton-meson interactions and that the effects of feedback from the $J/\psi$ itself are minimal. Additionally, we observe that shadowing has a substantial impact on the $J/\psi$ yield compared to absorption, thus we argue that the presence of shadowing is crucial to maintaining quantitative agreement with experimental data, in particular, with regards to the steeply increasing $J/\psi$ yield at the beginning of the reaction and the overall magnitude of the yield at equilibrium. Furthermore, we reveal that the application of the kinetic-rate method to heavier mesons such as the $\Upsilon(1S)$, where the effects of direct parton-meson interactions and shadowing are more pronounced due to larger parton-meson coupling constants, results in lower yields of these heavier mesons compared to $J/\psi$, thus we predict that the yields of these heavier mesons should exhibit similar increasing trends with nuclear collision centrality as observed for $J/\psi$. Lastly, we emphasize the necessity of incorporating transport methods that account for the influence of shadowing and absorption, in addition to equilibrium limits derived from thermal models, in order to accurately interpret the phenomena of parton-meson equilibration and quarkonia transport in nuclear collisions. Moreover, we emphasize the need to investigate the phenomenon of parton-meson equilibration with a particular focus on the interplay between direct parton-meson interactions and feedback from the $J/\psi$ itself. Furthermore, we emphasize the need to investigate the phenomenon of parton-meson equilibration with a particular focus on the interplay between direct parton-meson interactions and shadowing. Robots that learn from observations in real-world environments using inverse reinforcement learning can face obstacles when experts' demonstrations are marred by extraneous data from their surroundings. This unwanted information is usually eliminated in controlled settings, but when impossible, it needs to be filtered out. However, tracking down the source of this extraneous data is a challenging task, especially with large amounts of data. A new approach utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian model to analyze both expert and extraneous data, effectively acknowledging the diverse range of observations a robot may encounter. By distinguishing between two types of observations - those that contribute to a task and those that don't, this model can provide more accurate representations of tasks. In our experiments, we demonstrated that incorporating this learning framework into a MOGAN architecture outperformed other methods in a simulation scenario, closely mimicking the complex settings of unstructured environments. This model can be applied to a variety of situations, including scenarios where objects are picked up and placed in various locations. Given a subgroup $H$ of the fundamental group of a space $X$, we develop the concept of a strong $H$-SLT space by adapting the definition to the relative version. This extension allows us to investigate the existence of a covering map for these spaces, and under certain conditions, a semicovering map can be regarded as a covering map when the space satisfies the strong $H$-SLT property. Our study further explores when the whisker topology coincides with the lasso topology on $\widetilde{X}_{H}$, and examines the correspondence between open subsets of $\pi_{1}^{wh}(X,x_{0})$ and $\pi_{1}^{l}(X,x_{0})$. We also provide illustrative examples to demonstrate the validity of our findings. Moreover, we establish that every strong $H$-SLT space satisfies the $\mathbb{Q}$-$H$-SLT property, and discuss the relationship between these concepts, including the existence of maps that are locally homeomorphic to lasso fibrations. Finally, we find that every strong $H$-SLT space can be transformed into a space with the weak $H$-SLT property after imposing additional group homomorphisms. These contributions enrich the understanding of group-valued path spaces and provide new insights into the topology of these spaces. They also have applications in group-valued closed paths and Feynman integrals. Our study is particularly relevant to its applications in the context of Modern Physics, as exemplified by the Feynman integrals of gauge groups and Chern-Simons theory. A key insight gained from this study is that even though the Whitney topology does not always coincide with the lasso topology, our mapping techniques allow us to lift any Whitney local lasso fibration to an actual covering map. This proves to be a challenging open problem in the field and our study provides a significant breakthrough in resolving it. Furthermore, our study shows that the Whitney and lasso topologies are equivalent for spaces with the strong $H$-SLT property, and our developed mapping techniques are essential in proving this equivalence. A significant contribution of this study is the establishment of new coverage maps that are crucial in Chern-Simons gauge theory and Feynman integrals. We introduce a multi-phased deep reinforcement learning strategy to overcome control issues in complex scenarios. The standard application of deep reinforcement learning, though efficient in handling high-dimensional control problems, faces limitations in dealing with problems possessing specific properties such as irregular rewards or dynamic sensitivities. To address this limitation, our approach divides the problem into two interconnected components: predictive dynamics analysis and goal-optimized planning. The predictive dynamics model learns to predict future states based on current predictions, allowing for the exploration of the system's dynamics. Subsequently, a goal-optimized planner leverages this model to identify the desired actions to achieve the desired outcome. By utilizing this two-stage framework, our approach can effectively handle control challenges that standard methods struggle with. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach on multiple control problems, including a rocket-powered vehicle navigating a quadratic potential field and a quadcopter maneuvering through a complex environment, both with unpredictable sensitivities and obstacle-driven navigational challenges. The success of our method is quantified by comparing it with alternative strategies, such as direct reinforcement learning, while also visualizing the predicted dynamics models to illustrate their accuracy. The source code for this work is available on GitHub at https://github.com/atchan2019/rllabCD. Furthermore, the associated video can be found on YouTube at https://youtu.be/7VMG1TKoBvM. By achieving an average reduction of 0.08 of the initial cost of direct reinforcement learning, our approach demonstrates improved performance without incurring significant additional computational costs. The observed increase in computational demand was minimal, amounting to approximately 0.2 miles per second. This significant enhancement underscores the value of utilizing our multi-phased deep reinforcement learning strategy to address the stated control issues. The process of supermassive black hole (SMBH) growth in distant galaxies is a topic of significant interest. Our study combines the power of high-resolution radio observations with detailed analysis of a comprehensive sample of 37 galaxies from a specific cosmic era. By leveraging the capabilities of the Radio Astronomy Array Data Centre's radio data, paired with archival Spitzer mid-infrared data, we gained insights into the SMBH growth mechanisms in these galaxies. The findings indicate that two primary processes contribute to SMBH growth: one is instrumental in channeling material from the galaxy's central regions, while the other involves the SMBH competing with stars formed through a specific process within less densely populated areas. The resulting theoretical model suggests that to accurately explain SMBH growth, placing restrictions on the movement of material from the galaxy's centre and the rate at which the SMBH feeds on surrounding material must be part of any theory. Our discovery is instrumental in explaining SMBH growth in distant galaxies and lays the groundwork for future studies of SMBH growth through radio and mid-infrared observations. The study also highlights the potential of future radio and mid-infrared telescopes to monitor SMBH growth directly by tracking the changes in these galaxies over time. The research is also making data and models available through the Radio Astronomy Array Data Centre's website for the purpose of transparency and to promote further study of the subject. As part of our effort to educate and engage the public, a video explaining the research and its significance is available through the ABC's iView platform. Additionally, to bring the research to a more accessible level, a version of the article is available without technical jargon on the ABC Science Online platform. Lastly, to promote collaboration and communication among researchers, a meeting to discuss the research and related topics was organized by the Radio Astronomy Array Data Centre in collaboration with the Australian National University. During the meeting, the participants exchanged ideas and provided feedback on each other's research and discussed the potential of future radio and mid-infrared telescopes to monitor SMBH growth directly by tracking the changes in these galaxies over time. Deep neural networks can create versatile learning models for translating data and relating it to relevant properties. However, in various scientific fields including inelastic neutron scattering, deep neural networks face challenges such as limited availability of labelled data, difficulty in quantifying uncertainty in results, and the complexity of understanding their workings. To tackle these problems, we employ various techniques. Firstly, using simulated data, we train a deep neural network to differentiate between two possible magnetic models of a half-doped manganite compound. Secondly, we apply a novel deterministic method to provide accurate probability ranges for the classification, which highlights the importance of incorporating realistic instrumental constraints during the training phase for reliable analysis of experimental results. Finally, by analyzing the network's decision-making process through class activation maps, we determine which data segments hold the most influence on the network's final classification outcome. Our study showcases the effectiveness of combining advanced machine learning methods and in-depth data analysis to derive definitive conclusions in complex scientific datasets. Our approach is expected to greatly contribute to the analysis of data in neutron scattering experiments as well as in related fields such as X-ray scattering and muon spin resonance. Over the past thirty years, preprints have undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly shifted from physical to digital distribution. Preprints enable rapid and low-cost online dissemination of research findings to a broader audience within a matter of days. This work provides an overview of the evolution and influence of preprints within the scientific community over the past three decades. The analysis reveals a substantial 6300-fold increase in preprints within this time frame, albeit only accounting for a modest 4% of published research. The benefits of preprints for authors are also explored, including earlier exposure to an audience by an average of 14 months and significantly higher citation rates at five times that of non-preprint articles. To alleviate concerns over preprint quality, data shows that approximately 41% of preprints are eventually published in peer-reviewed journals with publication outlets being of equivalent influence to papers lacking preprints. The critical role of preprints in communicating emerging research during recent public health crises is also underscored. The quantitative findings presented may serve as a template for evaluating the impact of preprints in specific fields and could be used to advocate for preprints in deciding submission criteria. The hope is that by quantifying the preprint movement's effects, this work will foster a deeper understanding of the role of preprints in modern scientific communication. Moreover, the insights gained will guide the development of preprint systems that are better aligned with researchers' goals and requirements. Ultimately, by understanding the past, we can design the future of preprint distribution and utilization to best serve the needs of science. To this end, we also offer recommendations for enhancing preprint accessibility, streamlining distribution processes, and promoting preprints within various scientific fields. Our goal in presenting these proposals is to ensure the continuity and growth of preprints for another thirty years. Our vision is for preprints to remain an essential and influential component of global communication in the years to come. By remaining cognizant of preprints' history, we can create a future where their potential is fully harnessed. Our proposal for preprints' future is one where these documents continue to drive scientific progress, facilitate collaboration, and make research accessible to a broader audience. Our hope is that the insights presented will guide the development of preprints into an indispensable tool of contemporary science. By analyzing the preprint movement's effects, we aim to identify key lessons that will steer preprints into their most beneficial possible applications in the years to come.

In contemporary laboratory settings, meticulous research data management is crucial. Multiple available solutions are either highly tailored or require substantial modification to be effective. This paper introduces a unified solution designed specifically for data-driven investigators working individually or in small groups. Our electronic lab journal is generated automatically and includes detailed entries, as well as annotated images, linked files, and experimental outcomes captured in real-time using smartphones with built-in microscopes. This seamless workflow is facilitated by our smartphone-based microscope system, which is calibrated to provide precise imaging measurements. Furthermore, we describe a novel algorithm for accurately scaling up images while maintaining object-to-image focus alignment. This innovative system enables laboratory staff to concentrate on actual research, while our software seamlessly captures and documents experimental data and processes images in the background. This effective laboratory management system is currently being used by our group, comprising twelve members. It's essential to note that this solution is not proprietary and is completely open-source for the benefit of the scientific community. Any interested researchers can modify or simply replicate our methodology to suit their requirements. High-entropy alloys, prized for their remarkable strength and flexibility in their composition, are gaining significant attention due to the unexplored possibilities they present. Yet, unlocking their underlying physics to create new and innovative HEAs poses a significant challenge, mainly due to the inherent complexity of their chemical properties, making theoretical modeling difficult and requiring vast databases to analyze candidate materials. Artificial intelligence (AI), specifically machine learning (ML), has the potential to overcome these hurdles by its capacity to handle complex relations. This comprehensive review will delve into how ML is effectively used in modeling and designing HEAs, highlighting areas where simulations succeed in predicting materials' mechanical and physical properties with remarkable accuracy. Additionally, it will outline the existing limitations of simulations and propose potential pathways to mitigate them, thus paving the way for further research in the field. It is anticipated that this summary will provide a thorough understanding of the utilization of ML in HEA simulations, encouraging scientists to contribute novel approaches and encourage collaboration to create artificial intelligence that aids in creating next-generation high-entropy alloys. In this context, "artificial intelligence" and "machine learning" will be used interchangeably. In the context of our discussion, "high-entropy alloys" will refer specifically to binary, ternary, quaternary, and beyond solid solution alloys with a high degree of entropy, whereas "transition metal" will be used to refer to elements classified as transition metals according to the standard periodic table classification. Lastly, "AI-driven" materials design will be the standard nomenclature for materials design facilitated by artificial intelligence. The measure of a vector-valued function's nonlinearity is essentially its deviation from affine functions. Researchers have proposed and refined hypotheses about a specific bound for this nonlinearity; Liu, Mesnager, and Chen initially proposed a general upper limit in 2017, which Carlet later supplemented with a lower bound using differential uniformity as a reference point. Our research refines this existing lower bound using straightforward methods. To accomplish this, we establish a new type of set, termed "Sidon sets," and demonstrate that vector-valued functions whose images lie within these sets have significantly reduced nonlinearity values. We also identify the "Sidon dimension" of affine functions, effectively giving us a criterion for evaluating and limiting the maximum possible nonlinearity values. Although our work's parameters are currently the most optimized we know of, we hypothesize that the bound can be further refined. As evidence, we provide a specific function example whose parameters achieve this lower bound plus one. Using similar reasoning, we also refine existing upper bounds on vector-valued functions' uniformity and differential uniformity, ultimately proving them to be identical and significantly lower than general partial spread bounds. Our work is further exemplified through numerous vector-valued function examples, which demonstrate the correctness of our proposed bounds. Additionally, we provide a general approach for automatically searching and finding functions with optimal nonlinearity values and specific properties. Using this framework, we successfully discovered and verified a vector-valued function with 4-fold complexity and a significantly lower nonlinearity value compared to previously known functions. As an application of our research, we explore and explain the relationships between vector-valued function properties, ideals, and affine functions. Our work specifically incorporates and extends existing results from noncommutative algebra, as exemplified through the examples of Dujmova et al.'s function and Taniguchi's function. Lastly, we extend our research to multivariate functions by defining and applying generalized Sidon sets and ideals, ultimately deriving new bounds on vector-valued function nonlinearity and providing illustrative example functions. Our work significantly broadens the understanding of multivariate function properties and provides a framework for automatically searching these functions. Using this framework, we successfully discovered and verified a vector-valued function with 4-fold complexity and a significantly lower nonlinearity value compared to previously known functions. Our research further refines existing results by providing multiple generalizations and new bound results for vector-valued function properties, as well as provides a new understanding of generalized ideals and their applications to function properties

Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research and analyzing them is essential for identifying complex patterns. Researchers use various methods, such as comparing real data with simulated data that adheres to a null hypothesis. Our work involves exploring the space of binary matrices that fulfill specific row and column sum constraints, which differs from the uniform sampling methods that previously existed. Instead, we modified two existing algorithms that switch elements based on non-uniform probabilities assigned to each entry through a weight matrix. Our results indicate that including zeros in the weight matrix can create issues, but specific cases with monotonic structure can still yield reliable outcomes. Using simulations and a well-known bird habituation study, we examine the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms and the importance of choosing an appropriate null model for accurate data analysis. Integrating diverse sets of data, including data on the transverse momentum distribution of D mesons and semi-inclusive processes involving both D and $\bar{D}$ mesons, into the fitting process of parton distribution functions (PDFs) has been a challenge due to a lack of comprehensive theoretical predictions. To address this, we have developed a procedure to generate theoretical predictions that take into account the integration of partons into hadrons, while also accounting for the effects of fragmentation and the potential biases of observables sensitive to the momenta of parent partons. Applying this to data from LHCb on the double-differential cross-section of the interaction between neutrons and D mesons, our analysis utilizing the NNPDF3D PDF set reveals the integration of the D dataset increases the precision of the fit by approximately $4\%$ and also causes a notable shift, of approximately $1\sigma$, in the position of the modulus of the parton distribution of the valence quark $d$. Furthermore, our calculations demonstrate the cross-section of the interaction between neutrons and D mesons is expected to be approximately $8\%$ higher than previously estimated at a momentum of $80\,{\rm GeV}$. Finally, our study reveals the potential for future experiments to measure the momentum of parent partons to an accuracy of approximately $4\%$. We've investigated parametric seeding in microresonator frequency comb systems to enhance output stability and adjust frequency comb properties. Our study, which involved a fixed microcomb locked to a laser reference, focused on the parametric seeding process and its effects on the microcomb's spectral characteristics. We found that applying parametric seeding led to a combination mode selection mechanism, which stabilizes the output field and offers the ability to adjust the frequency comb's pattern and shift. Notably, as the driving power increased, the output field's purity improved significantly, ultimately resulting in a high level of stability similar to that achieved with non-pump spectral lines. Our findings also led to the development of a simplified method for frequency comb tuning. To demonstrate the practical applications of this technique, we successfully aligned a microcomb with a fixed laser reference and then re-tuned the microcomb to match a laser whose frequency changed. Our experimental results showed that this method allows for smooth and stable management of microresonator frequency comb systems undergoing frequency fluctuations. To date, the fastest known auto-frequency locking of a microcomb has been achieved, with a line narrowing rate of 42 GHz per second. Our research not only expanded our understanding of parametric seeding but also paved the way for advanced microcomb applications. We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following points:

  1. A clear illustration shows how linear co-adding techniques can fail to maintain a well-defined point spread function, especially when weighting varies significantly between frames.
 2. A requirement for linear co-adding algorithms to maintain a well-defined point spread function is identified as the necessity for all pixels to be illuminated by a constant signal contribution throughout the exposure period.
 3. An analysis of the Raab co-adding algorithm reveals that it fails to maintain a well-defined point spread function due to its reliance on an unmodified weight function that can cause light to diverge from its original position.
 4. A novel and optimal Raab weight function is derived that ensures constant signal contributions and thus maintains a well-defined point spread function. This optimal weight function is shown to be identical to the widely accepted mean-weighted Raab algorithm for cases of uniform exposure.
 5. A device code for implementing the optimal Raab algorithm is provided, along with demonstration images showcasing its effectiveness in maintaining a well-defined point spread function. This code can be used even when individual exposure times vary significantly. Moreover, a related Python package is available for use in astronomy research and data analysis. Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, being a crucial component derived from the short time Fourier transform (STFT). The traditional approach focuses on the maxima of spectrogram peaks. Recent research has shifted towards exploring minima and zeros, revealing links to Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs). Despite these connections, theoretical analysis of GAF zero sets remains challenging due to their complex stochastic structure. Statistical methods applied to spatial data are used but primarily understood empirically. This work explores the geometric stochastic structure of spectrogram level sets, providing rigorous theorems that explain their distribution. This new perspective offers potential innovative methods for spectrogram-based signal detection and estimation. This study demonstrates the feasibility of its findings through various signal processing applications, including detection, filtering, and signal recovery, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of spectrogram-based methods. The underlying mathematical concepts may also be useful for analyzing Gaussian fields on general triangulations. In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological orders are frequently encountered.  The study of these orders is complicated by the fact that the wave functions of flat band states are highly localized on specific lattice sites, making it difficult to identify the underlying mechanism driving their correlation.  To address this challenge, we employed the exactly solvable lattice models - the Hubbard model on the kagome lattice and the one-electron tight-binding model on the cubic kitelattice - to investigate the correlation properties of their flat bands.  Our analysis revealed that the short-range correlations associated with these bands are significantly weaker than those found in the extended states.  The observed decrease in correlations is attributed to the localized nature of the wave functions, limiting the influence of site connections.  The resulting implications of this finding on the intensity of interactions within flat bands are also explored.  The findings of our research could be used to evaluate the stability of flat bands in real-world materials.  By doing so, the connection between flat bands and their associated correlation effects can be fully understood.  Furthermore, the distinct correlation characteristics of extended states within these systems were identified.  The differences between the behavior of flat bands and extended states were then used as a basis for developing a generalized distinction between the two.  The distinction was then applied to the one-electron tight-binding model on various lattice configurations and used to identify criteria for constructing flat bands with controllable interaction properties.  The findings of our research could be used to design materials hosting strong interactions with flat bands,  potentially using artificial structures such as holographic surfaces. The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane orthogonal to their collective movement across the sky. 

Using the sample of wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) and considering effects from large angles, simulations indicate a relatively low uncertainty of around 30 meters per second in velocity measurements when line velocities are taken into account, rather than projected sky velocities with an uncertainty of around 100 meters per second.

However, analysis based on using the line velocity method, with additional steps to eliminate potential anomalies by identifying and discarding 2 times standard deviations from the mean, reveals that no distinct deviation from Newton's gravitational law exists at a radius of around 10,000 astronomical units. 

Due to the relatively low uncertainty in velocity measurements, existing wide binary star data have nearly sufficient accuracy to differentiate between the principles of Newton's gravitational law and the Modified Newtonian Dynamics model using the line velocity approach. In contrast, to make the same distinction with projected sky velocities, data for around one thousand additional wide binary systems will be needed.

Furthermore, to accurately determine how gravitational forces work in this context, potential sources of systematic error must also be accounted for, including any hidden or unobserved companion stars within these wide binary systems and possible moving groups within these star systems, with control being achieved statistically by narrowing down and considering specific and well-established groups such as the Pine cone cluster, the Wolf 1628 group and the ELDEN star group. 

Finally, to make any future findings reliable and free from bias, data for wide binary star systems should be obtained from observations made without any prior assumption based on previous studies, but rather through statistical analysis of the actual data without any influence from previous findings.

Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, multi-source satellite data streams often have varying missing data
rates and errors, making precise AOD estimation and prediction challenging.
Therefore, a practical need exists to develop a physics-based statistical method
for wildfire AOD forecasting by integrating heterogeneous satellite data streams.
By incorporating spectral analysis, the proposed method merges multiple satellite
datasets with an underlying advection-diffusion model, treating each dataset as
a transport of AOD "tracers" over time and space. This method is demonstrated on
three California wildfires using data from two satellites, MODIS and ABI, operated
by NASA and GOES, respectively. By incorporating NLDAS soil moisture data as an
external factor, the method is shown to produce more accurate and complete AOD
forecasts than solely using satellite data, especially in extreme wildfire scenarios.
The resulting AOD predictions are validated against ground-based AOD measurements,
yielding a 20% reduction in mean absolute error when using single-dataset models.
Ultimately, the integrated method provides more reliable AOD predictions than
existing error-prone statistical methods and offers valuable implications for
using multi-source satellite data in various applications. The method has been
implemented in an open-source Python library, PyADFS, accessible for public use.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within a specified boundary. The framework's efficiency is shown in an artificial and real-world scenario. Artificially, we generated interdependent location data and assessed our proposed framework against actual location data from the New York Taxi Dataset. Real-world results show our method can maintain a certain level of privacy while maintaining usable map views with our tool, MapPrivator. This tool ultimately allows data owners to set a privacy threshold and adjust the map view according to that threshold without compromising it.
