Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on signal processing techniques, the authors propose using a higher-order statistical method called the fourth-order cumulant to identify abnormal heart conditions.  Compared to previously studied methods, the proposed approach demonstrates improved noise robustness and variability tolerance.  To evaluate its effectiveness in real-world applications, the authors recorded 15 seconds of cardiac auscultation sounds from 100 subjects using three different devices, including stethoscopes, electronic diaphragms, and a smartphone-based device.  The sounds were then processed using time-frequency analysis and feature extraction techniques to identify mitral heart conditions.  Performance results show that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing signal processing techniques, with an improved accuracy of 14% and 12% respectively, on noisy diaphragm recordings and stethoscope recordings.  Future work will involve collecting more data to improve the proposed method's performance and accuracy.  The authors also plan to conduct clinical trials to assess the effectiveness of these techniques in real-world applications. This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human bidders purchase an exclusive good, we assess the impact of a credible and uncredible auction environment on bidding behavior. In auctions that can be manipulated, we discover that the majority of bidders adhere to the strategy of submitting a fixed price bid. Notably, in uncredible auctions, bidders tend to engage in more aggressive behavior, leading to significantly higher prices relative to credible auctions. Our findings suggest that the credibility of an auction format can significantly influence bidding behavior and, ultimately, affect its performance and revenue generation capabilities. Building on this insight, we propose a novel approach to assessing the integrity of double auctions as a benchmark for evaluating market mechanisms. This test can be used to compare the performance of different market mechanisms and determine which ones can be considered reliable and efficient. Our research also expands on the understanding of double auctions, contributing insights into bidder behavior, auction outcome efficiency, and the potential for market mechanisms to be influenced by participants' perception of the auction's integrity. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/5CvOYnoHvG8. Finally, the paper will conclude with potential future applications and directions for further investigation. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Our novel approach, "Variable Extension for Local data Retrieval" (VELER), enables sequence index length customization by designing two opposing PCR primers. By combining our DNA-storage system with VELER, we've established a state-of-the-art infrastructure for local and remote data storage and retrieval, demonstrating the real-world feasibility of practical DNA-based storage solutions. Experimental results corroborate the theoretical advantages of our proposed methodology over existing DNA storage methods. A quantum algorithm is described that successfully estimates the Shannon entropy and von Neumann entropy of a discrete, discrete-continuum probability distribution, running in $O(\poly(N, \log M) \cdot 2^{n/2})$ time, where $N$ represents the number of possible outcomes, $M$ is the range of the continuous variable, and $n$ is the number of qubits used in the quantum computation. This algorithm leverages two previously proposed methods for calculating entropies, modifying them to account for the case where the probability distribution is not uniformly distributed, and includes the possibility of knowing only the support of the distribution. The assumed access to this distribution is random, possibly after having accessed a known source of entropy in the distribution. The algorithm is shown to be compatible with distributions that have logarithmically sized supports, and it is anticipated to be efficient when the entropy of the distribution is known to be large. The possibility of modifying this algorithm to calculate other entropies, such as conditional entropy, is also explored. Additionally, a related algorithm is proposed that can generate uniform random variables from any given discrete or continuous probability distribution in the distribution's support in $O(\poly(N, \log M) \cdot 2^{n/2})$ time. This capability to sample distributions is known to be essential in various fields, and it is shown here that it does not impact the running time of the entropy estimation algorithm. Finally, quantum algorithms for estimating entropy in scenarios with multiple variables are proposed, utilizing the access to individual variables one at a time, and dependent on the known entropy of each variable in turn. The proposed algorithms are shown to be efficient for small qubits, and it is shown that the known entropy sampling bias can be corrected, resulting in improved sampling quality. The efficiency gains come from the knowledge of entropies, and it is shown that the proposed algorithms can estimate entropies while remaining sampling efficient. The quantum algorithms for sampling and entropy estimation presented here are the first of their kind, and they offer the first known quantum methods for these tasks. They also compare favorably with known classical algorithms in terms of running time and sample size. Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples. Additionally, it establishes a connection between linear strain vanishing properties and almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes. Specifically, it proves that a specific linear strain vanishing property holds for these complexes, including the particular case of the Straffin-Sullivans' $k$-vector ideal $I_{k}$. The paper further examines the linear strain ideal $I_{\sigma}^{1}$ associated with any pure dimensional simplicial complex $\sigma$. This is accompanied by computational tools to assess the Cohen-Macaulay property of simplicial complexes and ideals using a software called CoMaCS. This program can determine if a given monomial ideal is almost Cohen-Macaulay, as well as analyze the rank of a matrix formed by binomial coefficients. For example, it can confirm the almost Cohen-Macaulay property of the ideal $(x-y)^{3}(x-y)^{2}z$ in $R=\mathbb{Q}[x,y,z]$. The CoMaCS software is available for download at https://macs.mapsgis.upr.edu/CoMaCS.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. Additionally, we demonstrate a data-dependent bound of $O(N^{2/3}K^{2/3})$ for the number of quantum gates. Given the rapid advancement of quantum technology, the potential for quantum-driven breakthroughs in machine learning is increasingly plausible. Moreover, the utility of these algorithms is maintained even when the datasets are too large for classical methods, offering a future possibility of efficient machine learning on massive datasets utilizing quantum computing. Finally, the evaluation of algorithm performance using data-independent and dependent metrics provides an opportunity to evaluate the efficacy of quantum machine learning for various tasks. Based on our findings, the development and testing of more advanced quantum algorithms, such as neural networks, are worthwhile pursuits, offering the potential for future breakthroughs in machine learning. We also introduce and evaluate a quantum algorithm for supervised learning, incorporating the utilization of classical data to inform quantum algorithmic decisions, thereby enhancing their performance. The quantum algorithm's dependence on data dimensions is comparable to classical methods, requiring $O(N^{2/3}K^{2/3})$ applications of qubits and quantum gates. However, it outperforms classical methods in terms of processing efficiency, allowing it to scale more smoothly with an increased number of data points. Nonetheless, the efficacy of this algorithm is subject to the same limitations as K-means, potentially causing it to become trapped in local minima. To address this shortcoming, we modify the algorithm to incorporate a mechanism for escaping these suboptimal solutions, thereby ensuring global optimality, at the cost of increased computational requirements proportional to the square root of the number of data points. Furthermore, the utility of these quantum algorithms for solving larger problems than their classical counterparts poses an opportunity to evaluate their effectiveness in a variety of tasks.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an innovative approach that leverages analysis-based point visibility prediction to accelerate visibility-aware differentiable rendering, achieving superior shadow quality and improved speed. By utilizing triangle indices instead of per-pixel normals for visibility evaluation, our method significantly outperforms existing shadow approximation techniques, achieving visible-over-occlusion consistency while maintaining rapid computation at up to 60 frames per second on a single GPU. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to two challenging image-based inverse problems: shadow removal and single-view 3D reconstruction. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method demonstrates improved results in enhancing user experience during visual data exploration. We've conducted an empirical assessment to validate these findings. The benefits of this interface include reduced cognitive load for users, as they only need to specify minimal natural language context to access relevant entity properties, and the ability to handle large datasets with ease. Conversely, the primary challenge lies in efficiently handling cases where multiple entity properties match the user's input, thus potentially overwhelming them with information. To address this limitation, the implementation includes a utilization-based ranking system that assigns weights to entity properties based on user behavior and their established links within the Linked Data framework. As a result, the modified interface demonstrated improved performance, as demonstrated by our experiments, and users can specify entity properties and generate diagrams more efficiently. We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design is characterized by a fundamental tradeoff between flexibility, quasisymmetry, and nested flux surface volume. We also introduce a new metric to characterize stellarator modular coils and utilize this metric to analyze the essential features of stellarator design. Our findings validate the importance of integrating integrability objectives to maintain quasisymmetry properties during coil flattening. Furthermore, we show that our design strategy can accommodate varied stellarator sizes through scaling. Lastly, we discuss the computational efficiency of our approach and outline potential avenues for further research. Our work presents the first step in a comprehensive algorithm that can facilitate a wide-ranging stellarator design exploration. A detailed description of this algorithm's various subroutines is provided in a companion document. We also maintain an open-source code repository for our design tool, which is documented in another document. Our design tool is specifically tailored to address three fundamental questions in stellarator design. Firstly, can quasisymmetry be achieved through analytical designs? Our analysis indicates that, under the current design methodology, an ideal (error-free) design from NCSX is already significantly distorted, let alone the NRCF design. This suggests that, with the current design approach, quasisymmetry can be achieved but only up to a certain maximum rotational transform value. Secondly, can stellarator design be optimized for multiple rotational transform values? Our method demonstrates the possibility of designing stellarators for multiple rotational transform values and even surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume in these regions. Lastly, can stellarator design be optimized while accounting for coil placement as well as various design metrics? This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most minimal form of map functions that maintain submersion properties. It's demonstrated that the b-principle can be applied to this type of map function, thereby including submersions and breaking down into simpler map functions like double coverings and covering substitutions. A key method of proof involves utilizing the efficient approximation of oriented colored broken submersions and developing novel control on approximation errors. Our findings also suggest that m-principle could be achieved for oriented colored broken submersions under specific conditions. Our research may be applied to solving a range of problem types, including the Bertrand-Dierkes problem and issues related to the uniqueness of intrinsic graphs in domain expansion. Two additional articles are set to explore further applications of these theorems. One article will delve into the Bertrand-Dierkes problem, while the other will investigate the uniqueness of intrinsic graphs in domain expansion and explore other related problems. It's anticipated that the content of these articles will be more comprehensible with the understanding of the present material. This research was initially presented at the research seminar at University of Montreal during the spring and summer quarters of 2019, with additional presentations at the Severi series at the University of Montreal in November 2019, the summer school on geometric partial differential equations at the PDE group at the University of Madison in July 2019, the summer school on partial differential equations at the analysis group at the University of Verona in August 2019, and various other mathematical conferences. Concurrent research by E. Stepanov on the approximate representation of map functions with properties of submersions to m-principle has yielded comparable results. Our approach, however, takes a distinctly different outlook, with an efficient and precise form of approximation having been achieved without the need for inductive arguments or the usage of approximate lapse functions. Instead, geometric invariants of map functions have been utilized in developing the b-principle, with corresponding results also being found for map functions involving colored points and b-principle variants involving min-principle and m-principle. In addition to these contributions, this research also establishes a novel link between approximate representations of map functions and first-order partial differential equations, thereby yielding findings of importance in this field. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov solvers and BDDC/AMG preconditioners is employed to tackle the resulting system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to assess the impact of multiple factors on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. These factors include different algebraic subdomain solvers, BDDC algebraic solver choices, various algebraic multigrid methods, and three-dimensional finite element grid constructions. Furthermore, a detailed study is conducted to optimize the BDDC method by selecting the most effective options through extensive experiments. Cardiac mechanics problem simulations are carried out using approximately 1,260,000 and 51,272 finite elements, allowing for a rigorous evaluation of the two preconditioners. Our investigations have shown that BDDC exhibits superior performance when compared to AMG on the given problems. A significant advantage of BDDC lies in its potential for substantial speedup and memory savings over a straightforward AMG implementation. To facilitate further research, a set of parameter values leading to a promising balance of efficiency and effectiveness for the BDDC algorithm has been documented. Additionally, a study is initiated to investigate the scalability of BDDC on large-scale heart tissue models. These types of models are used to simulate the mechanical properties of heart muscle using a reduced representation of its structure. Using a reduced number of elements, 8.1 million finite elements, a further examination of BDDC's performance is conducted through a comparative study with AMG. A notable finding shows that BDDC offers a notable improvement over AMG when solving problems of this scale, indicating its great utility for large-scale cardiac mechanics simulations. As a result, BDDC is seen as an indispensable tool for investigations of heart muscle tissue on a large scale. Altogether, this research suggests that BDDC is an essential tool for thoroughly studying the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue on various finite element grids of different scales. Our investigations have not only provided significant insights into the subject, but they have also laid the groundwork for future research in this field. As such, this knowledge can be applied to a wide range of related problems in computational mechanics, where solving large algebraic systems is of paramount importance.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. However, the main limitation of current numerical assessments based on the linearized Euler equations is that they require substantial computational resources due to the explicit formulation of acoustic variables. To overcome this challenge, this research proposes a novel high-order discontinuous Galerkin method on unstructured meshes to efficiently simulate 2D acoustic waves and control their manipulation by bianisotropic metagratings. By utilizing a conservative and stable discretization scheme, acoustic wave propagation is accurately simulated, and these numerical findings are then applied to determine the optimal design of a thin bianisotropic metagrating for an effective waveplate conversion at 250 kHz. The proposed method demonstrates a significant computational speedup (up to 50 times) while achieving a detailed resolution of acoustic variables. This innovative approach offers a versatile tool for the numerical design of acoustic devices and provides a foundation for the development of efficient meshfree methods. Additionally, acoustic wave propagation data are presented for the elected metagrating design at 250 kHz. Lastly, the research introduces an innovative fractional time-step technique for spatially decoupled acoustic pressure and particle velocity solvers. This approach contributes to the development of efficient algorithms for solving nonlinear acoustic equations and provides a foundation for extending the successful discontinuous Galerkin method to second-order Eulerian fluid dynamics simulations. The proposed temporal technique is applicable to any higher-order scheme and is not limited to acoustic simulations. It can be adapted for simulating heat transfer and other transport phenomena subject to parabolic PDEs within the context of fluid dynamics. The newly established time-step strategy offers considerable computational efficiency (up to 20 times) by isolating and solving the nonlinear Euler equations' pressure field independently of the particle velocity. This innovative approach paves the way for the efficient numerical resolution of the Euler equations' nonlinear acoustic phenomena. Consequently, this research lays the groundwork for the development of efficient meshfree methods, contributes to the advancement of efficient time-step strategies, and facilitates the numerical design of acoustic devices through the simulation of wave manipulation. The proposed numerical methods not only simplify the computational analysis of acoustic interactions but also significantly accelerate it while achieving precise numerical convergence. This breakthrough sets the stage for exploring novel numerical methods for simulating physical phenomena, notably for electromagnetic and photonic applications. Moreover, this work opens up new possibilities for acoustic metagrating design through computational optimization techniques and offers promising avenues for simulating nonlinear acoustic phenomena, such as acoustic shock

Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we manage to enhance this rate to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Under the condition that the frequencies are sufficiently low, by incorporating the principles of the Littlewood-Paley theory, we find that the solutions have properties belonging to certain Besov spaces of negative order and establish the most favorable $L^2$ decay rate. Moreover, combining the principles of the nonlinear energy method, similar to those employed in the Navier-Stokes equations, we prove that the solutions possess certain higher regularity and achieve the best $L^2$ decay rate. Ultimately, we establish the existence of the steady-state solutions using the standard energy method, by first deriving some important a priori estimates. Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers a promising way to develop flexible and high-density networks. Mobile IAB, which facilitates the connection of UEs in motion, holds potential as a suitable solution. This work takes a different approach from existing literature by Mobile IAB by leverging frequency-reconfigurable surfaces to enhance the performance of IAB links serving mobile UEs. Mathematically complex issues are addressed by developing an optimization framework that maximizes the sum of IAB links serving UEs on a roadside infrastructure, utilizing reactive IAB power control and surface reconfigurable control. The proposed framework is a computationally efficient method that takes advantage of the convexity of the objective function to minimize interference and optimize IAB link performance, which are confirmed through simulation results. This approach is seen as a promising way to enhance the performance of IAB links, which are known to have limitations in terms of data transfer. This, in turn, can improve the overall quality of service (QoS) of IAB-based networks. Next steps could involve exploring IAB link reliability as a primary objective and investigating IAB link vector perturbations. The latter could be achieved by utilizing multiple frequency reconfigurable surfaces and assessing the interference caused by IAB link activity. This could be done through numerical studies that account for IAB link packet transfer and the variability in IAB link data transfer rates. Finally, the potential of meta-learning techniques should be investigated for their potential to improve IAB link data transfer efficiency and flexibility in IAB network management. This could be achieved by leveraging recent advances in the meta-learning of IAB related variables and parameters. The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that the non-radiative condition leads to a formulation of the electromagnetic momentum that is consistent across all inertial frames, and subsequently explores the electromagnetic momentum in terms of a charge and its associated non-radiative electric and magnetic dipole moments. The calculation reveals that the electromagnetic momentum is entirely accounted for by the momentum of the charge's electric dipole moment, with the magnetic dipole moment contributing only a scattering momentum that is negligible in comparison, and that the electromagnetic pressure exerted by this momentum is shown to be far exceeding the pressure associated with the charge's magnetic dipole moment, which is however still much smaller than the pressure associated with its electric dipole moment. The paper further addresses the energy density contributed by the electromagnetic field, which is often referred to as 'dark energy', revealing it to be many orders of magnitude weaker than the pressure associated with the electric dipole moment. Lastly, the paper uses this analysis to calculate the energy and momentum of plane wave photons, which is a long-debated area of quantum electrodynamics, and demonstrates that the conventional de Broglie relation is consistent with the non-radiative condition, although it does not adequately represent the momentum of a charge coupled to a quantum electromagnetic field. This is evident from calculating the average momentum of a charge coupled to a quantum electromagnetic field in a vacuum state, which is zero, and contrasts with the implications of the conventional de Broglie relation. Additionally, the paper notes the significance of the non-radiative condition in the context of Dirac's equation for spin-1/2 particles, and notes that while a similar condition may exist for the momentum of a spin-1/2 particle, it is not known at present. Finally, the paper uses the non-radiative condition to formulate a theory of gravitation, in which the momentum of a mass is coupled to a quantum gravitation field, and demonstrates that the gravitational pressure contributed by this momentum far exceeds the pressure associated with the mass's electric dipole moment, although the ratio of this to the mass's magnetic dipole moment contributes a pressure many orders of magnitude weaker still. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles prevent its widespread adoption in truly open-world settings. Most reinforcement learning solutions struggle to adapt to changing environments, address actions with large real-world consequences, and ensure accountability when making decisions that affect people's lives. To overcome these challenges, developing policies that minimize losses under uncertainty is crucial. We investigate the feasibility of such policies through the lens of robust optimization and multi-objective decision-making, allowing for a comprehensive exploration of the complex trade-offs involved. By employing tools like Frugal Gradient Estimation, Online Learning from Data, and Counterfactual Mean Field Optimization, we can tackle these challenges effectively. The proposed approaches demonstrate promising performance on complex tasks like Air Traffic Management and serious games like Stratified Fog of War, showcasing a notable improvement of 16% to 105% compared to established methods. Our novel evaluation metric, Success Vector, provides a thorough assessment of the success rate across various trade-off levels, offering a substantial 10% to 50% improvement in overall performance. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/argminion/RFLOW. In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more precise opinions. For retinal analysis in particular, recent advancements have led to increased use of multiple imaging methods: standard two-dimensional fundus photographs and more detailed three-dimensional imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography. Our study employed three distinct multimodal data fusion strategies centered on deep learning to tackle challenges in retinal analysis: early combination, intermediate fusion, and hierarchical integration. Noting that early and intermediate fusion approaches typically fail to exploit information shared by different data sources to their full extent, our hierarchical method focuses on fusing characteristics from various dimensions within a network, while also uncovering connections between disparate datasets. We implemented these strategies on classification tasks involving glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy using a mix of public and proprietary OCT-based datasets, which demonstrated that our hierarchical method performed optimally and laid the groundwork for improved diagnostic procedures. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks. By limiting model complexity and focusing on relevant images, this method reduces overfitting and improves dependability. Comprehensive experiments were conducted across multiple datasets to verify the hypothesis that X-ray images contain critical features indicating severe COVID-19 symptoms. Our results show that the proposed approach yields a moderate improvement in accuracy when compared to the baseline method, and that additional context is required to effectively identify patients at high risk, suggesting that the original hypothesis is only partially accurate. Furthermore, several challenges and difficulties in relying on deep learning models for predicting severe COVID-19 symptoms are highlighted, and areas for future improvement are identified. We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, Q(x))$, where $\Omega$ is a ball of any dimension. The functions $u$ and $v$ satisfy the equations $u = \lambda v $ and the transmission equation $v = \lambda u $ on $\Omega$. Assuming the medium's properties are uniformly positive and symmetric, we derive asymptotic estimates for $u$ and $v$ using variational principles, which yield specific lower bounds for their $L^2$-energies. The results are further extended to other spaces, which give rise to associated eigenfunctions. The findings, including the bounds, are established for $L^2(\Omega)$-solutions as well as $H^1(\Omega)$-solutions. The study also includes a discussion of known results, including those concerning the direct and inverse problems, and concludes with the characterization of "single-mode" solutions, which are those with only one non-trivial transmission eigenfunction. The analysis shows that in a radially symmetric medium, the $L^2$-energies of transmission eigenfunctions increase asymptotically, with their associated wavenumbers, which implies that only one eigenfunction can be non-trivial for large wavenumbers, thus making the "single-mode" solutions the only possible ones in such media. However, this contrasts with the behavior observed in certain anisotropic media with "single-mode" solutions absent. Nonetheless, the solutions are found to be connected through their mutual dependence and the first transmission eigenfunction is found to be connected to the second by the equation $u^2 = v^2$. This mutual connection, with the first eigenfunction acting as a kind of " mediator", has significant implications for the direct and inverse problems by allowing the reconstruction of the second eigenfunction, and hence the medium's properties, from the first eigenfunction. This finding is further extended with the study of Dirichlet conditions, in which the first eigenfunction can still be utilized to determine the second eigenfunction, and thus the medium's properties. The study concludes with the analysis of a numerical experiment, in which various methods for determining the second eigenfunction, and thus the medium's properties, are demonstrated and validated. In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups. This upper limit surpasses the previously established bound by Neumann and Sims in the 1960s and also exceeds the revised bound by Mendes-Linares et al. in 2021. Furthermore, our work facilitates the computation of the number of subgroups for specific finite groups, with the exception of Coxeter groups. This exception remains an open problem in the field. As an alternative approach, we present a simplified version of Mendes-Linares' method for calculating the number of subgroups in a finite group. Using this simplified method, we successfully determined the number of subgroups for dihedral groups and quaternion groups. Lastly, we establish a general inequality to describe the exponential growth of the number of subgroups in a finite group with increasing order. This new inequality surpasses the previously established bounds by Hall and Valckenar in the 1960s. Additionally, we successfully applied this inequality to determine the asymptotic behavior of the number of subgroups in dihedral groups and Suzuki 2-groups. Notably, our results are in line with the conjectured general theory of group subgroups, which was first introduced by myself in 2019. This theory posits that the number of subgroups in a finite group should be $r^{\frac{\log_2r}{2}}$ multiplied by a polynomial expression with degree not exceeding two. This paper delves into the challenges posed by Visual Relationship Detection (ORD), a task that involves identifying relationships between objects in images, in the context of deep learning representations. Past research has highlighted that deep learning-based methods face difficulties in distinguishing between real and false positive data points, leading to data-driven biases in classification results. To address this limitation, our study uses pseudo-labeling - a technique allowing the assignment of labels to unseen data points - to overcome the restrictions of relying solely on expert-labeled data. By combining pseudo-labeling with regularization strategies to mitigate the associated risks, such as data pollution by inaccurate labels, we have developed an innovative approach to ORD. By applying iterative cycles of model refinement, coupled with data selection based on confidence levels and calibration metrics, we are able to improve ORD performance while effectively managing the impact of noisy labels. Notably, our proposed framework has demonstrated superior performance on three public challenge benchmarks (CORDS, Visual Relationship Detection, and TUIE), including a significant 9.2% improvement in mAP performance on CORDS. Our associated codebase can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/SunGouXu/Iterative-Refinement-for-VisualRelationshipDetection.

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone that outperforms state-of-the-art models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified error margin for MCM results. Our proposed ILP models for various MCM configurations are available in an open-source tool, integrated with the FloPoCo VHDL code generator, providing a complete flow from coefficients to hardware design. Thorough experiments were conducted to assess the models, followed by a detailed analysis of how to effectively apply sequential techniques to further improve the circuit area. These techniques were then used to optimize a practical application, showed to be feasible in FPGAs, including a challenging instance of MCM(8, 1024, 0.985). The proposed approach demonstrates the largest area savings of 41% compared to the state-of-the-art, saving over half the area for most MCM instances. For certain problems, a PTAS exists when the graph's structure satisfies specific conditions. To achieve a PTAS, certain graphs need to be simplified into more manageable forms while preserving the problem's solution. A significant challenge arises from ensuring that the simplified forms accurately reflect the original graph's structure, particularly for subgraph projections which may introduce errors. To overcome this limitation, certain graphs need to be further transformed into more reliable subgraph forms that can accurately capture the original graph's structure. In this context, we examine the feasibility of developing PTASs for specific problems on graphs with limited degrees and restrictive clause patterns in the underlying hypergraphs. To this end, we introduce a new concept of 'dual forms' for the constraints, allowing us to rephrase the problem in terms of the original graph's edges. This approach enables us to develop a new simplification technique that has the potential to yield a PTAS. However, a major challenge arises from ensuring the quality of the solution, particularly for the case of Matching, where the properties of the dual form are insufficient to guarantee a satisfactory solution. This approach enables us to develop a new termination criterion and derive a new inductive hypothesis, ultimately yielding a PTAS for the specific problems on graphs with limited degrees and restrictive clause patterns in the underlying hypergraphs. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic parsing task. Specifically, these models make use of linear projection matrices to transform query and key vectors in self-attention, thus introducing a learned prior for the syntactic dependency parser. In contrast to UPOA, UPIO includes an option to add linear projection matrices for the value vector. Our findings indicate that both models achieve success in the syntactic parsing task without relying on any pre-specified syntactic structures. Moreover, when combined with a self-training approach, these models reach new levels of performance in the Universal Dependencies framework across 36 languages. Notably, the models with the enhanced version of UPIO achieved better results than UPOA in 35 out of 36 languages. In particular, the models were capable of identifying basic sentence components including SVO order, as well as more advanced structures including relative clauses and sentences with multiple clauses. To evaluate their performance in the classification of grammatical functions, the models were adapted to recognize a range of functions including doer and recipient. Our study demonstrates that the models can identify grammatical functions with a high degree of accuracy for many languages, even when no prior knowledge of these functions is available. In addition, the models were applied to the tasks of sentence classification and sentiment analysis, as well as to the generation of sentences with modified semantic meanings. High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application of HSI, specifically focusing on detailed object classification in complex urban environments. By analyzing an HSI in multiple spectral bands, each object can be identified based on fixed frequency range associations. This simple, data-driven approach allows for efficient classification of complex scenes. Our analysis demonstrates that, unlike conventional RGB images, HSI signals provide distinct and distinctly related features for object classification. Experimental results, obtained from a drift-free dataset, showcase the efficacy of this technique, outperforming an established deep learning method that relies solely on RGB data. Moreover, by treating each HSI band as a separate input channel, we expand the spectral range for classification tasks. This research offers a straightforward, yet effective strategy to exploit HSI potential, setting a baseline for more sophisticated frequency range-based methods. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/IndigoTeam_HH/HSI_Segmentation. Additionally, our team's website, https://indigoteamhh.github.io/, provides an overview of the team's activities and projects.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph moduli space. We establish a scenario in which the integrals are sign-definite and demonstrate that they share a connection with hyperbolic geometry. Specifically, we show that they align with certain integrals of Kleinian surface hyperbolic geometry previously studied by Mackey. Lastly, a comparison is made between the cohomology of the general linear group and the first real cohomology of the metric graph moduli space. Our evidence suggests that a significant majority of real cohomology in the graph moduli space can be explained by the general linear group. Our analysis also proposes the hypothesis that all real cohomology in the graph moduli space may be explained by the general linear group. This is supported by our observation that the first real cohomology of the metric graph moduli space shares a connection with Kleinian surface hyperbolic geometry, particularly through the locus of curves with a single nodal singularity. This is further substantiated by our computation of the first real homotopy group, which is found to be isomorphic to the first rational homotopy group. This calculation extends previous results by Mu\~noz and Parra to all genera. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through analysis of latent variables that RNNs primarily utilize their recurrence to identify background information, which is subsequently used to improve the reliability of object representations and facilitate categorization.  Additionally, our results revealed that background information can be effectively extracted by RNNs even when they are only activated partially, thereby offering an efficient explanation for the performance superiority of RNNs over feedforward models in cluttered environments.  We refer to this phenomenon as the 'cost of background information' factor.  Further experiments validated the key contributions of both horizonal and vertical recurrence in leveraging background information to support object categorization.  This study thus highlights the unique benefits of utilizing recurrent connections in artificial neural models for mitigating the challenges posed by cluttered visual environments. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system, instead resulting in a uniform charge distribution across the lattice. Furthermore, we observed that interactions can transform a point of transition from a non-Hermitian skin effect to a Hermitian mode counting effect, while altering the system's phase. Quasi-one-dimensional systems were also examined, with findings indicating that interactions can change the point of transition from a non-Hermitian topological transition to a Hermitian topological transition. These studies provide insights into the effects of correlations on the topological characteristics of non-Hermitian systems. They can serve as a reference for future research on the related topic of electron interactions in topological non-Hermitian systems. Our work paves the way for an expansion of correlated topological physics to encompass a broader spectrum of systems characterized by synthetic dimensions, symmetry, and interactions. As future goals, we aim to investigate systems characterized by multiple synthetic dimensions, as well as those with more intricate symmetry patterns. Moreover, we look forward to developing and detecting topological states of matter that are robust against interactions, which can be observed in both Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems. Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the consideration of tested non-standard interactions. The results from this analysis provide the most restrictive limits to date on the Higgs boson width in the standard model and its interactions with electroweak vector bosons. Additionally, the observed data are consistent with the standard model predictions in the Higgs boson width and its interactions with electroweak vector bosons. The observed 1σ sensitivity in the Higgs boson width is 0.4 MeV, 0.4 MeV, 0.5 MeV, 0.5 MeV, 0.6 MeV, and 0.7 MeV for gluon-fusion production of the Higgs boson in the low and high energy regions, respectively. Similarly, the expected 1σ sensitivity in the Higgs boson width is 3.5 MeV, 3.3 MeV, 4.3 MeV, 4.3 MeV, 5.3 MeV, and 6.3 MeV for gluon-fusion production of the Higgs boson in the low and high energy regions, respectively. The results from this analysis extend to carry out similar analyses in the fermionic decay modes of the Higgs boson, specifically the tau-plus-tau-minus and muon-plus-muon channels. The constraints on the Higgs boson width in the fermionic decay modes are more stringent than in the four-lepton final state analysis, and the results align with the standard model predictions in the Higgs boson width and its interactions with electroweak vector bosons. The set $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}+{\mathcal{W}}}$ comprises integers $x$ such that $0 \le x < MN$ for some multiplier $M$, which can be represented as the sum of a number from $\mathcal{S}$ and a number from $\mathcal{W}$. We are particularly interested in the function $R_{\mathcal{S}+\mathcal{W}}(x)$, which counts the occurrences of $x$ in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}+{\mathcal{W}}}$.

This conclusion deviates from the commonly observed growth rate $\sim MN^2/2$ in the classic Chowla's conjecture, where we compare two partition functions, $\Lambda(M,N)$ and $\mu(M,N)$, counting distinct representations and all possible combinations, respectively. Our result implies that $\Lambda(M,N) \sim \mu(M,N)/2$. Both parts of our proof build upon prior work by Tao and Tao/Ji, incorporating insights from ergodic theory and Lebesgue measure calculations. Moreover, our method yields an efficient algorithm for computing $\Lambda(M,N)$. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. A universal approach to calculating transitivity degrees is proposed by establishing a connection between the geometric and arithmetic properties of these varieties. Additionally, this study introduces a new concept: minimal semi-free actions. It is proven that a toric variety admits a minimal semi-free action if and only if it has a specific, highly structured set of orbits. This set is shown to be in one-to-one correspondence with the one-dimensional subgroups of the torus. As a result, the transitivity degree of any quasi-affine toric variety can be determined precisely. Finally, this study discusses the transitivity degree for other specific algebraic varieties, such as homogeneous spaces and linear spaces, providing precise or bounded estimates in each case. By combining these calculations with the recently discovered finite generation theorem, the transitivity degrees for the majority of these varieties are now known exactly. This study includes detailed examples to illustrate the applicability of these methods in specific cases. It also raises questions and makes conjectures about the geometric and arithmetic properties of algebraic varieties, offering a framework for future research in this field. A key goal for future work is to expand the existing results from Number Theory to a broader range of algebraic varieties, such as perhaps those involving non-quasi-affine toric varieties, homogeneous spaces, and linear spaces. In particular, this research specifically addresses the transitivity degree for the moduli space of curves of genus 2, by establishing that the transitivity degree is at least 3, and offering a reasoned explanation for why it may likely be exactly 3. We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation. In contrast to model-free Reinforcement Learning, which often requires extensive data collection to achieve comparable results, our model-based method proves to be more efficient and adaptable, allowing it to successfully transfer controllers between related but different environments with minimal tuning. Our work also provides a practical comparison of various constraints and theoretical analyses of the proposed concept's robustness and usability. Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between scheme metrics and the underlying arithmetic properties, allowing for scheme construction via linear combinations that achieve optimal performance. This approach is expanded to include various sequence types and applied to the distributed computation problem, yielding optimal performance with minimal communication strain, outperforming existing alternatives in some cases. This framework's potential extends beyond caching and computation to other network problems where sequence properties can be leveraged. Additionally, this paper discovers novel links between polynomial properties and important combinatorial objects like combinatorial designs and covers. This connection enables the construction of certain combinatorial designs with optimal properties, potentially increasing their perceived value. A broader exploration of the relationship between sequences is also conducted, investigating questions of equality, inequality, and upper bounds in the context of combinatorial objects. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive interpretation of the Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, offering an alternative to Escard\'o's choice-free selection monad. Additionally, we compare our method with other attempts to handle non-terminating processes, including the minimalisation operator and bounded quantification. While these alternatives work within a constructive and predicative framework, we find that the lifting monad offers a more versatile solution, and ultimately, a more accurate reflection of the original PCF semantics. We also discuss existing challenges in formalizing fixed point recursion and discuss two possible strategies, but conclude that both approaches pose significant problems. Ultimately, we hope that our work will facilitate further exploration of programming in predicative and constructive type theories, even when faced with non-terminating processes. Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without compromising safety or accuracy. Further testing is planned using actual robots to validate the method's performance in real-world settings. Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis. One area, non-selective text summarization, involves generating a brief summary of a given text without requiring the identification of key information. Two key methods for assessing text summarization are sentence similarity and sentence relevance, with similarity often determined by measures such as cosine similarity and sentence embedding or by indicators like position, length, and lexical similarity, and relevance by methods like sequence-based comparison and summary-boundary recognition. Our research focuses on solving this text summarization problem using a graph-based approach in which nodes represent sentences, derived from a graph model that incorporates sentence similarity, and edges represent connectivity, determined by sentence relevance. An edge is weighted with a value between 0 and 1 by means of a similarity metric. Node weights are calculated through a similarity metric, and a threshold is applied to retain only significant nodes. An edge is removed if its weight falls below the threshold, and a graph component is obtained. Subsequently, a time-series approach is used for node ranking within the graph component, and the top-ranked nodes are selected for inclusion in the summary. An external metric is applied to assess the quality of the obtained summary. Experiments using the CNN/DailyMail dataset yielded a state-of-the-art performance with a BLEU-4 score of 35.89, surpassing the 35.84 score achieved by SummarText. An analysis of various parameters, including graph density, was also conducted. Further study is recommended to address the problem of summarization without sentences and to explore the use of graph models with multiple edges per node. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation. This method involves Gröbner basis variables assignment, signature analysis and management, point filtering, and Gröbner basis conversion. Validation techniques are employed to verify correctness and filter out incorrect results. Experimental results demonstrate the practical efficacy of this approach. In particular, this method outperforms ideal-based Gröbner basis algorithms in several studied cases, with execution times being significantly shorter. The proposed method provides a computationally efficient solution to a previously proposed challenge, yielding correct results in all tested instances. The method has been implemented in software and made available for public use. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show a clear increase above a binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ fit, and their transverse momentum spectra follow a similar trend as Au$+$Au collisions, involving a similar number of participants. We have determined the inverse slopes of the photon excess spectra at $285\pm53$(stat)$\pm57$(syst) MeV/$c$ and $333\pm72$(stat)$\pm45$(syst) MeV/$c$ for minimum bias and most central events, respectively. Moreover, we found that the photon rapidity density in Cu$+$Cu demonstrates a similar power-law behavior versus charged particle multiplicity observed in Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy. In particular, our measurements reveal a transition in the photon exponent with respect to participant number, changing from $n_{\rm part}^{1.25}$ to $n_{\rm part}^{1.18}$. Furthermore, direct photons account for about half of the total photon excess and follow a parton saturation model explaining the data between $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess and charged particle multiplicity. We have also determined that the ratio of $\pi^0$ to photon avoids the Lund prediction by at least a factor of 5 in the range of $p_T<4$ GeV/$c$, indicating the contribution of direct photons against hadronic contributions at low $p_T$. Hence, our results suggest the onset of quark-jet dominance at lower participant numbers and the disappearance of the photon exponent in heavy ion collisions. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up. The exco2(n,H) function also possesses an interesting independence property: the minimal value of exco2(n,H) occurs when n is roughly a multiple of the smallest k value. We compute the codegree squared extremal numbers for K3^3 and establish the asymptotic ratio of exco2(n,K4^3) to exco2(n,K3^3). Based on these findings, we propose a revised hypothesis for a generalized tetrahedron problem. The determined numbers are applied to solve two long-standing open problems: the asymptotic codegree squared ratio of K4^3 and K3^3 and the existence of K4^3-free hypergraphs with maximal codegree. Moreover, we determine the codegree squared ratio of K4^3 and K3^3 to be 1/2. Lastly, the proof reveals the presence of K4^3-free hypergraphs with maximal codegree that exhibit the conjectured structure of Turan's tetrahedron problem. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. By comparing these results with those achieved using the multiquadric method, we find that our approach often yields a more precise solution with fewer interpolation nodes. Additionally, our interpolation function can be implemented with linear memory usage and allows for linear computation time. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including their recently discovered density profile, distinct characteristics, and the implications for understanding particle diffusion near pulsars. We also provide a concise summary of the statistical analysis of a large-scale population of pulsar halos, which has led to a crucial discovery: their density profile is correlated with the luminosity of pulsar wind nebulae. We discuss the possible remedies to mitigate the discrepancies encountered in explaining gamma-ray measurements through diffusion models, including the possibility that a substantial portion of cosmic rays originating from pulsars are trapped within localized structures before being released back into the Galaxy's cosmic-ray population. We explore the potential of future gamma-ray telescopes, such as CTA, to significantly increase the number of pulsar halos that can be studied, which in turn will significantly advance our understanding of particle diffusion near pulsars. With a anticipated 10-fold augmentation in 2021, the ASTROGAM satellite is slated to provide crucial observations of pulsar halos in 2023, thereby possibly employing density-weighted analysis to reveal fine-grained diffusion features. Nonetheless, we anticipate that the total number of pulsar halos to be observed may still be insufficient to unveil certain pivotal aspects, such as localized spatial inhomogeneities, through statistical examination. Therefore, the forecasting model will be revised to account for future measurements, which are anticipated to provide crucial insights into diffusion at the pulsar scale, which in turn will significantly impact our understanding of cosmic-ray propagation in the Galaxy. This updated model will be essential in planning and anticipating the implications of future observations of a vast population of pulsar halos. With the anticipated number of pulsar haloes from the ASTROGAM satellite expected to be 120, against the 12 currently known, we are positioned to gain a much deeper insight into diffusion at the pulsar scale, which in turn will reveal important details about cosmic-ray propagation in the galaxy. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
The proposed method surpasses the performance of existing weather detection methods, demonstrating its efficacy through the accuracy of its semantic segmentation. 
Moreover, we investigate the effectiveness of different weather-classification techniques and explore other aspects of vehicle sensing systems, such as fog-density estimation and free-space detection. 
In conclusion, our study marks a significant advancement in the development of robust weather detection systems. Fog-density estimation is crucial for various applications including free-space detection, but it also presents a challenge as there are distinct ways to classify fog densities and their difference from other weather conditions is gradual. 
In this study, we tested several fog-density estimation techniques and evaluated their overall effectiveness against our proposed weather-detection method. 
The outcome of this evaluation confirms the superiority of our proposed method in detecting weather conditions. A detailed analysis of various evaluation metrics is presented, along with code accessibility on GitHub for reproduction of our results. Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Moreover, our findings suggest that scientists' interest in climate change does not simply mirror the public's but rather shows a more consistent engagement. Furthermore, our cross-influence model reveals that there is a two-way flow of influence between the public and policymakers, with a one-year lag, whereas there is no evident cross-influence between policymakers and scientists or economists, nor between scientists and any of the other groups. Lastly, our study discovers that climate change interest tends to experience seasonal fluctuations, tendentially, though these variations do not significantly impact our main outcomes. Ultimately, our model provides a framework for investigating the dynamic relationships within a system composed of multiple interconnected groups. By varying the groups included, our study demonstrates the feasibility of exploring cross-influence among any collection of entities with a clear and measurable area of interest. Conversely, our analysis also highlights potential challenges in capturing dynamic interests when (a) the groups of interest have little to no overlap with each other, (b) the signals underlying their interests are heavily embedded in noise, or (c) they exhibit little variation in the interest signals themselves. By investigating these difficulties, our research strives to contribute to an improved comprehension of dynamic systems composed of interconnected groups.
