Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In this study, a novel infinite-dimensional control method is introduced, combining the infinite-dimensional nonlinear control of heat conductive structures with an energy-based formulation. The developed controller can be applied to any heat-conductive gripper design, capable of being generalized through deep learning. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on a two-fingered gripper, showcasing successful grasping of complex objects within a simulated environment. The integration of this method with off-the-shelf 3D printing technology allows for the rapid prototyping and control of soft grippers with exceptional results. The proposed strategy has significant potential for optimizing soft robotic performance. One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when the gradient surface is complex. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods. The proposed method, known as the Lagrangian Natural Gradient Descent method, can be applied to a broad range of problems characterized by constraints and manifolds. The LGND method guarantees efficiency on convex problems and offers exponential convergence for specific non-convex problems. To validate the efficiency of this method, we performed comprehensive testing on various numerical simulations. The results confirm that LGND consistently outperforms NGD, often by a substantial margin, particularly when constraints are present. The proposed method also demonstrates significant computational savings, according to a scalability analysis. The presented research highlights the potential for the Lagrangian Natural Gradient Descent method to tackle a range of challenging optimization problems. The simplicity and ease of implementation of this method will likely extend its applicability to a broad range of applications. The method is predicted to be particularly beneficial in areas such as tensor networks and quantum deep learning, given their resemblance to Lagrangian formulation. Furthermore, the conceptual framework of the method could be applied to develop new gradient descent algorithms by combining the legacies of prior methods. The LGND method represents a crucial step towards creating a new class of optimization tools. This means that not only do CSOs, but also intermediate frequency peaked sources and quasars, play a significant role in the overall population of high-redshift active galaxies. Furthermore, young, high-speed objects such as Gigahertz-PEaked Spectrum Objects (GPS) are likely involved in the early development of black hole activity, whereas slow-speed compact symmetric objects signify the completion of this process. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating how healthcare professionals combine various sources of information to make accurate predictions. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 lung cancer patients. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the utility of visualizing individual patient characteristics through collaborative filtering, highlighting specific medical scan regions associated with high-risk patients. Interestingly, the results show that incorporating multimodal data significantly improved predictive accuracy, with the text-based clinical information having a greater impact than the visual medical scans. Follow-up research could involve incorporating rich audio information and using a more sophisticated attention mechanism to further refine predictions. By leveraging the strength of convolution neural networks in extracting spectral features, our method effectively classifies density perturbation types. Furthermore, by utilizing Gaussian processes as regression tools, our framework enables the precise reconstruction of acoustic oscillation patterns, enabling accurate determination of the matter density, sound speed, and Ricci curvature parameters. Through simulated data tests, our method demonstrates the ability to provide precise and consistent estimates of these parameters. Our results show strong promise, suggesting that future quasar spectra surveys may be able to constrain the parameters of our model to within a 5% margin of error. By integrating the constraints from future quasar spectra surveys with cosmic microwave background data, the parameters of our model can be precisely constrained to within a 1% margin of error. Our work presents an alternative to previously proposed approaches and highlights a potential new tool for determining the parameters of cosmological models. This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators. Our analysis also sheds light on the irreducibility of modules whose restrictions to $\frak m$ are one-dimensional. Furthermore, we conclude with a distillation of our key outcomes into a set of central prototypes involving Weyl algebras. Our study draws upon ad-hoc methods to address these problems, which might be of independent interest in the field of Lie algebras. Our work is partially inspired by Sugiyama's U(𝕙)-free modules and the work of of Tomiyama on modules of Douglas, in addition to Sun's result on the irreducibility of tensor products between modules of Kostov type. Our work also extends that of Bortola, Kozman, and Milusovic in connection to Lie algebras of differential type, with some of our results sharing parallels with Lim's work on generalized Virasoro algebras. Lastly, we include a collection of protocols that verify the irreducibility of certain modules free over $U(\frak m)$. One such protocol is Sun's result, which has applications to Lim's algebras of type VI. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The
project's source code and model weights are publicly accessible. Additional resources
can be found at the URL. https://github.com/tiezhengdev/role_constrained_dialog.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework that facilitates collective learning of a shared vocabulary among nodes within the system. This collective learning enables nodes to efficiently convey unique data patterns, leading to a significant reduction in required transmission bits. To effectively handle dynamic signal states, a neural signaling game solution is proposed, demonstrating improved performance compared to traditional methods such as maximum likelihood estimation and quantization. Simulation results confirm the benefits of this emergent language solution in transmitters, with nearly all unique data patterns being mapped to a single transmission bit when the vocabulary size is 128. This substantial reduction in data bits, equivalent to 99.9%, eliminates the need for extensive transmission and greatly contributes to the goals of minimal data transfer and ubiquitous connectivity. This solution is also adaptable and can be applied to a variety of scenarios, including both isolated nodes and networks, by incorporating a neural game framework with neural networks. A major advantage of this solution is the collective emergence of efficient communication methods that are robust to changes and can be easily shared among nodes. Additionally, the solution's focus on emergent language also contributes to the optimization of network resources, including power and bandwidth, by facilitating collective learning and cooperative behavior among nodes. This behavior is characterized by efficient, efficient, and cooperative characteristics. Moreover, the solution is compatible with existing standards and can be implemented using existing hardware and software capabilities. A comprehensive software platform, known as the ELG Semantic Communication System, has been developed to showcase the benefits of this innovative approach. The C++ based platform successfully demonstrated the effective connection of nodes within a system, as evidenced by a test case involving semantic connection between UEs and Base Stations in a 5G wireless system. Experimental results confirmed the efficient operation of the solution and the emergence of a shared vocabulary among nodes, thereby ensuring a reliable and efficient connection. Furthermore, the solution was successfully applied to a variety of scenarios, including both uplink and downlink transmissions and connectivities, and achieved a range of performance improvements, including significant reductions in data bits required for transmission and improved signal robustness to changes, through extensive testing and validation of the software platform and its capabilities. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate that this dimer behaves as an active colloidal particle, moving end-to-end in a particular direction, or becoming completely immobile in response to the gradient. Our analysis reveals that these two behaviors are accurately described by a dimensionless quantity measuring the ratio of the activity gradient to the particles' stiffness. Additionally, we outline a method to determine the dimer's effective activity coefficient in a uniform activity environment, which could be applied to other complex geometric configurations. This quantity is found to depend solely on the activity gradient and the dimer's shape, as well as its stiffness. This framework may also be used to study the movement of active micromotors and the response of active materials to external stimuli. Lastly, we have extended our theoretical predictions by incorporating a time-lag in the dimer's activity response, which leads to the development of sophisticated, complex-shaped dimer micromotors. This time-lag is shown to greatly influence the dimer's ability to maintain its end-to-end movement and can even cause a sudden reversal in direction, as well as a temporary reduction in movement speed. This behavior remains largely unchanged until the dimer's internal time-lag becomes comparable to the time-scale of the activity gradient. Furthermore, we observed that incorporating a time-lag also makes it possible to create dimer designs with nearly all-to-all asymmetry in their shape, which can still follow a straight line when moving. This capability is most likely to appear in dimer designs triggered by activity, or when they have a rigid T-shape structure. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of active dimer structures, whether they have internal rigid parts or their movement is controlled by a time-lag factor. Both scenarios share a common ground as part of a more extensive theory describing the dimer's response to activity gradients, or when their movement is dictated by flexibility factors, as previously explored in our previous research. This overall research aims to provide a unified framework for active dimer structures by combining their inherent geometry, external activity factors, and their inherent physical properties in a single, all-encompassing theory. This framework may also be used to study other complex geometric configurations, or when their movement is dictated by flexibility factors, as explored in our previous research on active dimer structures. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly reach the target formation, this approach first locates the target formation's heat source (equivalent to the median formation), then employs a registration process with contractive mapping to swiftly achieve the target formation, and finally, uses a gradient descent to fine-tune the formation and minimize the distance between the current and target formations. Simulation results indicate that the proposed strategy successfully evades obstacles, maintains a constant formation shape, and only requires slight adjustments after collision avoidance, thus reducing the time spent on reformation. To automate decision-making for the strategy, a performance metric called "collison avoidance quality" (CAQ) is devised, displaying the correlation between time and energy consumption following collision avoidance. The proposed approach's effectiveness is validated through realistic simulation experiments, and the associated source code is made available online. The research presented here provides insights into achieving collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms, setting the stage for subsequent studies to optimize the related problems. To this end, a list of unresolved challenges is provided. RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for a heterogeneous V2X network that incorporates RSUs, vehicle relays, and users. Assuming users are localized within M x M square areas, with their mobility generating Poisson point processes, and utilizing the effective six-coordinate representation of location, this method enables the derivation of precise analytical expressions for key performance metrics, including the coverage probability, relay selection success probability, and average system capacity, which can be utilized to validate the effectiveness of various techniques by comparing simulated and analytical results. Two strategies, relay selection with switching and a blended approach combining RSU and relay communication, are examined to confirm that the blended method yields superior performance in both coverage and capacity. To further enhance the accuracy of stochastic analysis in cases of restricted user location, a novel technique is introduced, allowing the integration of user density functions at the analysis level. This enables the analysis of approximate coverage and capacity performance in situations of limited location. Moreover, comparing the accuracy of simple bounds derived from this method with those from existing methods shows that these new bounds exceed the precision of currently available methods. Two techniques are proposed to improve the computational efficiency of analytical bounds, individual approximation and combined approximation, with the latter demonstrating a 90% decrease in computational complexity while maintaining less than 5% error relative to the exact value. In contrast, without these methods, an approximation error of nearly 100% is observed. To validate the efficacy of these methods in cases of severe congestion, numerical evaluations are conducted, confirming that the blended technique yields improved performance in both relay communication and coverage, and underscoring the necessity of accurately modeling location for accurate stochastic analysis. Moreover, the proposed bounds demonstrate exceptional precision, reducing computational complexity by a factor of 10 or more in some instances, which is far superior to simply bounding the log term. Lastly, examining the effectiveness of these methods in extremely confined locations reveals that a combined approach remains superior to relay communication alone, with an approximation error of under 20%, in contrast to an error of over 90% for the standard bound, underscoring the value of utilizing user density functions in stochastic analysis in these situations. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To address this issue, we have developed a new approach that combines neural machine translation models with attention mechanisms to better understand what editors look for when assessing articles. By applying this model to the task of identifying low-quality sentences, our results demonstrate a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art technique, showing a 15.8% increase in F1 score. Additionally, we examined the role of attention weights that guide human editors in deciding which sentences are of poor quality, and found that our model agrees with human annotations more than the previous approach, particularly on articles with technical content. Our hope is that the labeled dataset we created will aid in future research and contribute positively to the quality of Wikipedia. Based on our findings, we suggest that automatic systems such as our own be used to evaluate articles randomly to increase the percentage of articles deemed of high quality, and further propose that these evaluated articles could potentially be used as educational resources to instruct new editors. Finally, we recommend that these evaluated articles could potentially be used as educational resources to instruct new editors. Additionally, we recommend that Wikipedia's quality scale be revised to assess articles based on the quality of paragraphs rather than sentences. This could simplify the assessment process, increase overall quality, and provide valuable insights into what constitutes high-quality writing. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having the original network's training data and labels, which may not always be available due to storage or data access issues. This paper addresses the challenge by providing a way to create accurate student models even when only the original network's pre-trained weights are accessible, without needing the original training data. This is achieved by employing a novel two-stage approach called Discriminative Knowledge Distillation. First, a discriminative network is created to refine and select the most relevant features from the pre-trained network, using a previously unknown label set. Then, these features are used to train a compact student model through knowledge distillation. Experimental results show that this approach significantly improves the student's accuracy while still achieving a substantial compression rate. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and providing explicit, continuous-trace algebra computations for the resulting non-trivial Dixmier-Douady classes. Ultimately, we demonstrate that any solvmanifold can be represented as a $C^*$-algebra bundle of noncommutative tori, which we explicitly compute, while the monodromy of the original torus bundle is translated into a Morita equivalence among fiber algebras. Our findings validate the physical hypothesis that electric-magnetic duality is equivalent to a specific type of T-dual transformation. Additionally, we show that non-trivial, almost abelian solvmanifolds can be generalized to form non-trivial, non-torsion, and non-nilpotent examples solvmanifolds in higher dimensions. Our work is closely related to the research of Kalbus, Segal, and Wong on T-duals of torus bundles, which we extend and generalize. Our general T-dual framework is compatible with calibrations, which explains the concentration of differential forms in the dual algebra. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer demonstrations from multiple agents, either by seeking external guidance or through self-refinement, to create a unified policy that simultaneously benefits from both agent and peer demonstrations. Through the integration of two distinct knowledge acquisition methods - Knowledge Gradient and Experience Reinforcement Learning, CoIL's algorithm optimizes the interaction between knowledge acquisition and imitation. Thorough experiments conducted across multiple domains validate the superiority of CoIL's co-imitation learning approach. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. Furthermore, a novel test is developed to identify and connect units within a interference network. This interventional model and associated methods are applied to data from the Add Health survey, allowing for the identification and visualization of treatment interference clusters. Our findings indicate that units receiving treatment interventions from healthcare managers are central to interference networks, suggesting that extenuating actions can exacerbate interference in individual units. Our analytical approach and graphical tool for identifying interference networks are instrumental in understanding extenuating actions and guiding decision-making at the community and policy levels. 

To address practical challenges in working with interference networks, we have created a tool that uses a novel approach to identify central units within these networks. This method considers multiple factors such as treatment status, extenuating actions, and a unit's relationship with its surroundings to determine its central role in interference. Our analysis of the Add Health data reveals that units involved in extenuating actions are consistently central to interference networks, regardless of the radius of influence or statistical test used. This finding is consistent across various radii of influence and statistical methods. Our methods for identifying central units, detecting treatment interference, and visualizing interference networks are documented in R packages named Interference, Centrality, and InflUI, respectively. These packages are freely available on CRAN at [www.CRAN.R-project.org](http://www.CRAN.R-project.org). The ongoing success of weak-lensing research on the large scale structure of the universe depends heavily on accurate correction methods to remove biases in galaxy shape measurements. Our analysis provides a comprehensive picture of the shear bias spectrum for galaxies in the SDSS dataset using the meta dataset from the Kilo Degree Survey, which was analyzed with the ngmix software package. Through an analysis of 507,085 galaxies in the $0.05<z<0.30$ range, our results reveal a consistent trend of decreasing shear bias with increasing galaxy brightness. Utilizing an additive shear bias model developed by Hart et al. (2017) and incorporating corrections for edge effects, our findings demonstrate improved agreement with the theoretical predictions of the SHAPE pipeline. Additionally, our analysis highlights minor discrepancies between the observed shear and E/B-tiled biases. To facilitate further research, our study metacalibrates are made available to the community through the Meta dataset website. Our analysis also confirms that, after applying correction for edge effects, most shape noise can be eliminated, resulting in highly accurate alignment of the galaxies. For 299,576 galaxies in the $0.05<z<0.30$ range with signal-to-noise ratio greater than or equal to 5, the remaining shape noise after applying corrections is found to be less than $0.3$ percent. Our work indicates that, despite the presence of some residual systematic errors, our shape measurements are accurate enough for the determination of weak-lensing cosmological parameters. Our findings further suggest that further research should focus on eliminating small bias variations between adjacent fields to achieve final optimal cosmological parameters through weak-lensing studies. To achieve this, our study proposes the utilization of a weighted cosmology fit. For 299,576 galaxies in the $0.05<z<0.30$ range with signal-to-noise ratio greater than or equal to 5, the application of a weighted cosmology fit results in minimal variation of the shear bias spectrum, with less than $0.4$ percent variation in most cases. Our analysis demonstrates the utility of this approach in maintaining consistency of the weak-lensing cosmology fit, even with small biases. Our meta-calibrated shape catalogs, along with associated weight files, are made available through the Meta dataset website for the benefit of the research community. Our study also confirms the efficacy of the ngmix meta-calibration method for determining weak-lensing cosmological parameters, as demonstrated through a cosmological fit of the Kilo Degree Survey data using the meta-calibrated shape

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency. In particular, this TRNG achieves a maximum throughput of around 262.85 Mbit/s, while also generating random numbers with an entropy level of at least 99.97% as confirmed by the NIST randomness tests. In contrast to other state-of-the-art TRNGs, which either require a binary supply voltage, specific environmental conditions, or frequent reconfiguration, TuRaN is distinguished by its ability to operate continuously under normal conditions and the high quality of its output. As a result, this TRNG is suited to a wide range of applications, including, the security of devices at a hardware level. In particular, this TRNG can be utilized in the pseudorandom number generation needed for tasks such as encryption, by which it can reduce energy consumption by at least 95.81% compared to other alternatives. In addition to its usability in TRNGs, this paper also explores other possible hardware applications, such as, the generation of testing vectors, logarithms, and other binary values, for which it can reduce energy consumption and increase throughput. In order to accomplish this, we propose an approach, termed CoRaN, which enables the determination of circuit failures by sampling the circuit in a parallel manner and then using the SHA-256 hash function to identify these failures. In particular, this approach can increase the throughput of testing by three orders of magnitude, while also lowering energy consumption and latency

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine the case of a second-order loop diagram involving a three-body scattering process. Notably, the resulting causal representation exhibits characteristics similar to a finite section of a planar loop equation. Our findings indicate that the causal representation captures the underlying loop topology with exceptional clarity. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model.  An experiment was conducted across four sets of essay scoring tasks, demonstrating the superiority of BERT and RoBERTa-based models over an LSTM-based baseline in all areas.  Furthermore, our findings show that pre-training BERT and RoBERTa on a combination of relevant datasets is key to achieving high levels of accuracy in automated essay grading, often surpassing performance when these models are fine-tuned directly on labeling data.  An external set of development tasks was also utilized to validate the efficacy of these models, resulting in a success rate of 70.95% for BERT and 71.10% for RoBERTa.  Our model's performance in these tasks, coupled with previous research outcomes, suggests that transformer-based models are particularly well-suited to applications like automated essay grading.  Our hope is that these findings will guide researchers in this domain and contribute to further advancements in natural language processing technology. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To explore this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model assigns each person a random family based on the previous generation's social mobility, tracing generations in a vertical direction. Our model analyzes the effectiveness of educational opportunities in overcoming the inherent social mobility hurdles it imposes. The study further considers the social consequences of using genetic information to make decisions about access to opportunities, which can result in individuals being denied resources based on their family's background, a decision they may disagree with. Ultimately, the value of these opportunities is evaluated by measuring their impact on overall social welfare and the well-being of individuals throughout the population's vertical progression. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities. 
In other words, Delegated RingCT offers a suitable compromise between anonymity and transaction finality speed. 
Therefore, Delegated RingCT can be considered a suitable solution for DPoS-based cryptocurrencies that require anonymous transactions. 
Ultimately, Delegated RingCT aims to provide a more practical and feasible solution for enabling privacy in decentralised payment systems.

Our analysis reveals how this property impacts various categories of linear systems, including those defined by undirected graphs, which are particularly interesting because they can be solved in a linear amount of space even when the graphs are irregular. Additionally, if solving almost exact linear systems in a specific order translates to solving exact systems within a larger class of linear systems, this implies the ability to solve exact linear systems within that same class, which applies to undirected graphs regardless of their structure. Furthermore, almost exact methods for certain subclasses of linear systems, such as undirected graphs, also imply exact methods for these subclasses, which further extends to more general categories of linear systems. These discoveries lead to important insights and simple proofs, which have significant theoretical and practical implications. Our findings resolve the main question of Tal, Zwick, and Zwick's paper from 2018 and establish a more robust result, which also addresses an open question in the field of parameterized complexity, while additionally providing new insights and discoveries. Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise. An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples. The proposed SL-MPSF method is implemented using specialized solvers for safety constraint optimization problems. The associated software and data models can be found on our website. Ensuring a system's safe operation is a top priority, and safety-assured filtering technologies like the model predictive safety filter (MPSF) play a vital role in achieving this goal. Originally, MPSF was designed to monitor and correct system behavior while adhering to safety standards, but it has since been expanded to include various disturbances, including those with unknown origins [1], [2], and [3]. This paper builds upon those advancements and employs system-level synthesis (SLS) methods to create a new MPSF design that includes the most challenging type of disturbance, bounded disturbances. The primary advantages of our MPSF design over traditional MPSFs include a reduced number of adjustments to control inputs and fewer and less extreme corrections. We also propose a specialized variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability while requiring fewer online computations. These optimizations come at the expense of slightly more pronounced safety constraints. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated in numerical examples. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. We propose an alternative method to enhance the system's security by randomly altering the source phase to a more comprehensive degree. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task may not always ensure a high in-context learning performance for that specific task, especially when it comes to a few-shot setting, and that language modeling performance and in-context learning do not always correlate as one might expect. Our research also offers additional insights into the in-context learning dynamic by examining the influence of a pretraining corpus's style and the model's size, as well as the distribution of a pretraining corpus. Our findings could be especially useful to developers working on large-scale LLM development. Moreover, our model and corpora can be accessed via our website: https://incontextlearning.github.io.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are then used to develop synthesis models, and the effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through the analysis of subjective and objective scores on the Zerospeech 2019 challenge database. The results show that acceptable quality speech synthesis at a low bit rate can be achieved with the proposed units. The model's flexibility also allows it to generate speech with distinct regional accents by adapting existing monosyllabic acoustic units. The proposed approach has the advantage of not requiring manual segmentation or labeling, and can automatically identify and clustering useful acoustic units for speech synthesis. The model's efficiency in terms of bit rates is also demonstrated. The technique is versatile and can be utilized for modeling various types of transient and steady-state regions in speech. The speech synthesis system developed with this method outperformed the challenge baseline at a lower bit rate, and has the potential to be used for synthesis with distinct regional accents. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. It successfully planned multiple tasks on the robot, including maintaining an upright posture, making progress in the environment, and responding to external loads. Most of these plans could be executed successfully and showed a close match with the predicted trajectories. We've made the associated code and data publicly available. They can be downloaded from the repository https://github.com/ioros/McCormickEDL. Our current research focuses on integrating this planner with autonomous learning techniques to enable robots to acquire optimal gait patterns directly from sensor data. We're exploring applications of this approach in various real-world robotic challenges. For example, we've used it to help a hexapod robot climb a steep ramp while maintaining balance, see the video for more details. Additionally, we've developed a versatile simulation environment utilizing the Bullet Simulator, which allows for the creation and management of intricate multi-limbed robot simulations. This tool can be accessed through the GitHub repository https://github.com/ioros/McCormickEDL Simulations. We're eager to collaborate with other researchers, and our main goal is to make the developed methods and resources easily accessible and usable. We're confident that our optimization strategy, data-driven linkage technique, and associated projects can inspire new applications in the field of optimal control for robotics. We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource theories. The first method involves maximizing the achievable probability of transforming an input state into a desired output state. The second method involves minimizing the output quantum resource remaining after transforming an input state. We have applied these methods to various quantum resource theories, including maximally entangled states, quantum entanglement, and quantum work. The results we have obtained match existing theories for transforming quantum states in specific resource theories but also extend existing theories by providing more accurate descriptions of state transformations when the input state contains multiple copies of the same resource. We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques. This study investigates the optimal control issue of constrained nonlinear systems to balance performance goals with component life span limitations. To resolve this challenge, a specialized safety evaluation module is developed, which evaluates system safety in relation to performance outcomes. This safety module is based on two distinct parts: firstly, it determines a safe operating region to prevent damage; secondly, it calculates performance losses resulting from saturation. An algorithm combining model predictive control and multi-objective optimization is then proposed to achieve a compromise between safe and efficient operation. This algorithm is tested using a traction control system, which demonstrates its capabilities: when component lifespan is taken into account, the MPC algorithm prioritizes satification of traction and life safety constraints, thereby minimizing performance losses compared to systems with unlimited component lifespan. Moreover, when component lifespan is variable, the MPC algorithm adapts to optimize performance, while fulfilling traction and life safety constraints. In addition to the implementation of MPC, we show that a corresponding differential dynamic programming approach can be employed for real-time applications. This method's efficiency was verified in a experimental setup. Finally, the efficacy of these optimization strategies was validated through hysteresis band control. This approach's simplicity and robustness are highlighted as significant advantages. Relevant expertise includes that of MPC specialists, who have addressed a wide range of applications in control theory, and that of real-time software developers, who have solved problems related to scheduling and data transmission. As a result, these proposed control strategies are well-suited to practical implementation. Indeed, preliminary tests conducted on an experimental vehicle have yielded promising outcomes. We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula. This approach facilitates a visual and intuitive understanding of the confidence area's shape and size. Additionally, this method can be applied to related 'Lévy $\alpha$-stable' distributions, where the confidence area's shape remains the same but its size changes depending on $\alpha$. Furthermore, our method can also be extended to incorporate confidence intervals for sample statistics such as the mean and interquartile range. Importantly, these confidence intervals will always cover the true population values with a probability of at least $0.89$, as derived using a Monte Carlo simulation. In contrast, one-sided tests based on these sample statistics will have a validity of at least $0.89$ in these scenarios. In practical terms, this means that these confidence intervals and one-sided tests are almost universally valid, requiring only a probability of at least $0.011$ that the true values fall outside of them. Importantly, these results hold both with and without knowledge of the underlying distribution. In contrast, other methods, such as those employing asymptotic theory, provide little information about the likelihood that true values are included within the confidence interval. Nonetheless, our results suggest that these confidence intervals are most accurately applied when the underlying distribution is known to be Cauchy, as this is indicated by both the shape and size of the confidence intervals. In other scenarios, the confidence intervals will be less efficient. Notably, this can also be observed in the case of Lévy $\alpha$-stable distributions, where our method is almost as accurate as using the Fisher information, the optimal approach. In the limit of $N$ tending to infinity while the parameter $\gamma$ remains constant, the confidence areas shrink, approaching the shape of a $1/\sqrt{N}$-radius disc. Conversely, as $N$ increases towards infinity while the scale $\sigma$ increases towards infinity, the confidence areas expand towards a square with side length of approximately $\mu + i\mu + 2.5\sigma$, as the location $\mu$ becomes negligible. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across varying views and objects, while its geometric representation is also transferable to classification tasks. Furthermore, PRNet's keypoint network was found to outperform state-of-the-art methods in object detection on 3D datasets, highlighting its versatility. The proposed framework will likely influence object detection and registration tasks, and will likely prove beneficial in registration-based object detection pipelines. The PRNet code will be made available.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the vast number of possible appearances of objects and background in each image. Recent segmentation techniques that rely on semantic labels often assume a pre-existing segmentation of a limited training dataset, but this assumption is compromised when dealing with unlabeled modalities. Semantics-based models can, however, leverage additional context to improve their performance, such as when provided with segmentations of a different modality that can serve as a reference. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that capitalizes on the correlation between two modalities by training a model to synchronize their boundaries. Targeting segmentation of unseen imaging modalities, the proposed unsupervised instance segmentation method incorporates additional constraints that ensure boundaries are accurately aligned and object regions are correctly linked across modalities. The evaluation of the proposed technique on MRI-CT instance segmentation demonstrates superior outcomes when compared to a recently introduced segmentation technique that relies on cross-modality boundary alignment. The performance of the proposed method is further verified by processing CTSlices, an online, publicly accessible resource that contains human liver slices scanned in both CT and MRI formats. The presented 3D instance segmentation model can be accessed via https://github.com/alevazquez/SSD-UnsupSeg. The CTSlices experiments are documented in the appendix. Seminar presentations related to this subject can be found at https://alevazquez.github.io/SSD-UnsupSeg/. Seminar presentations related to CTSlices can be found at https://alevazquez.github.io/LiverSlices/. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on low-magnitude flares such as those from dMe, dMe, or M5e stars. In an effort to address this gap, we have developed a new automated algorithm to detect these low-magnitude flares and utilized this tool to analyze data from Kepler's short and long-campaigns, which enabled us to identify 282 previously unreported low-magnitude flares. Furthermore, our findings confirm that the flux distributions of these low-magnitude flares align with the pattern observed in intermediate-flare datasets, which suggests that these low-magnitude events are likely the lower limits of mild stellar flares. In addition, our analysis of 20 low-magnitude flares observed in three M5e stars reveals that these events often display double-peaked light curves and point towards a magnetic twist reconnection model as the mechanism that drives this type of flare. Lastly, our detection of 282 low-magnitude flares from over 150 different stars provides a new benchmark for evaluating the performance of future space missions such as the Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission and the James Webb Space Telescope. This new standard calls for observing low-magnitude flares with a precision of $\sim 10^{-3}$ in flux and $\sim 1$ minute in timescale. This new benchmark will help assess whether these future space missions are capable of accurately determining the total UV emission from low-mass stars during stellar flares. In turn, this information will enable a more precise evaluation of the potential biosignatures and habitability of planets in low-mass stars' environments. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as shearing after rotating), then we outline general strategies for verifying the reliability of these transformations in each category. Next, we adapt these strategies to be compatible with popular types of point cloud models, thereby forming the core of our security protocol. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using a variety of complicated 3D objects and a popular type of point cloud model called DGP, by validating its capabilities on a variety of frequent three-dimensional transformations including stretching, rotating, and a combination of both. DGP is particularly well-suited for this task as it includes implicit surface reconstruction capabilities that allow it to accurately detect both stretching and shearing. Additionally, our method's efficiency makes it suitable for use in frequent three-dimensional transformations such as those found in vehicle navigation. It's worth noting that while some of these types of attacks may seem unrealistic given the scale at which they occur, they can still pose a significant threat at smaller scales as demonstrated by our analysis. Temporal knowledge graph reasoning has emerged as a leading approach for
understanding complex event and temporal graph data. Building on successful
applications of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in static graph settings,
this study investigates the use of GCNs for temporal knowledge graph reasoning.
However, GCNs' reliance on simultaneous node input makes them inapplicable
to temporal knowledge graphs, which are often represented as sequences of graph
versions at different time points. To address this challenge, the study
introduces the ConceptualGCN, a novel deep learning architecture for temporal
knowledge graph reasoning. ConceptualGCN comprises a temporal message-aggregation
module that enables GCNs to reason about temporal knowledge graphs by iteratively
processing individual graph versions and combining conceptual messages from
earlier time points. When paired with the CE-GFWS evaluation metric, which
specifically assesses event temporal relationship reasoning, ConceptualGCN
demonstrates a notable 5.06% relative improvement over the then-best result on
the TKG-Bench2 benchmark. Furthermore, ConceptualGCN achieves state-of-the-art
results on various evaluation metrics across multiple benchmark datasets,
including TKG-Bench2, TACoS, TACoSv2, and VideoQA, thereby validating its
efficacy in temporal knowledge graph reasoning. Source code is available at

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, the acoustic properties of the ground can generate a sound wave when struck by an object, which may or may not be audible depending on the ground's properties and the listener's location. This research introduces a new method for simulating the sound produced by the ground after an impact, using a finite element approach based on the Rayleigh-Love equation for thin plates. By analyzing the sound produced by the ground under different acoustic conditions, it becomes clear that three factors influence its perceptibility: the coefficient of transmission, the sound speed in the ground, and the mass per unit area of the ground. To determine the optimal parameters for a realistic sound synthesis, an objective quality metric known as the mel-frequency cepstral distance is used, alongside a subjective testing procedure. A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this system with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Ultimately, the critical temperature's limitations stem from the vanishing hydrogen influence on the Fermi level states, predominantly controlled by boron's p states. Consequently, substantial amounts of hydrogen-like states near the Fermi level are essential for attaining significant superconducting critical temperatures in such hydrogenated monolayers. Moreover, our study delves into the potential of other two-dimensional hydrogenated compounds, demonstrating that those with hydrogen-like states near the Fermi level, such as H2O2, exhibit promising electron-phonon interaction and, by extension, significant superconducting critical temperatures. Conversely, the critical temperatures of H2B2, HB2, and H2B, also possessing hydrogen-like states, are substantially lower, primarily due to weak bonding between hydrogen and the other elements. Hence, these systems hold no promise as superconducting two-dimensional materials. Conversely, co-doping of hydrogen into existing two-dimensional materials like MgB2 could possibly yield notable improvements to their superconducting properties. Various research opportunities and challenges are also presented for further investigation. Lastly, the overall analysis underscores the pivotal role of hydrogen's influence on Fermi level states for attaining notable superconducting critical temperatures in such hydrogenated two-dimensional materials.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered critical errors previously unaccounted for in more conventional evaluations, thereby significantly enhancing the reliability of automotive safety-critical systems. To detail this process in greater depth, we provide a comprehensive case study outlining our step-by-step approach in applying formal verification to assess the robustness of highly automated driving systems. This extensive analysis serves as a valuable resource for experts striving to implement sound and reliable logical evaluations of automotive systems at a higher level of automation. Additionally, a publicly accessible verification framework along with formally defined specifications from our case study are being made available for the benefit of the scientific community. This is with the aim of promoting the use of formal verification across the industry, as previously established best practices are inherently limited in their capability to verify complex logical failures at a higher level of automation. It is hoped that our work in this domain will inspire the development of innovative methods for safety-critical evaluation of highly automated driving systems at a higher level of automation. It is further anticipated that our work will serve as a foundation for the integration of formal verification in the ISO 26262 revision process currently underway. This is with the aim of providing significant and lasting improvements to the standards set forth for automotive safety-critical systems. This is in recognition of the capacity of formal verification to safely ensure the robustness of complex logical failures at a higher level of automation. To facilitate widespread adoption of this approach, we have made our verification methodology and the associated framework publicly accessible for the benefit of the scientific community. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that accounts for temporal change. This method utilizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence to a non-fixing global reference frame, adapted to the systems' natural oscillations. Demonstrations are performed on simulated data, power grids with time-varying parameters, and datasets from the IEEE Council on Electric Power Systems and the MIT Research Society, showing a high success rate. This approach can be applied to a wide range of dynamic clustering problems. Additionally, a discussion is provided on adapting this method to deal with missing data and dynamic systems following power law distribution. This research has been funded by the French National Institute for Health and the French Agency for Research and Evolution. Based on this study, a MATLAB tool called Dynamic Cluster, is made available for researchers to apply this method to their data. This tool can also be used for manual analysis and has been utilized in previous studies on segmentation, synchronization, and clustering of time-series data. Some of these studies include the determination of default risk levels by identifying groups across various credit rating agencies, dynamic detection of electrical disturbances in power transmission systems, and the detection of functional groups in gene expression profiles using multiple species. These studies have contributed to advanced data analysis in medicine, power systems, and bio-science. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, the distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle. Furthermore, our work confirms that the infinitesimal method is compatible with the fundamental principle of the exchange principle. In contrast to SIA, however, our method does not preclude the use of transcendental or 'unbounded' infinites, and does not conflict with the generalised Leibniz rule for differentiating products. In particular, our method is distinct from SIA in its treatment of the product rule, and is more faithful to Leibnizian notation. In terms of its philosophical implications, the Robinson-based SPOT is an attractive choice, as it is the only method that can be used in a real-valued, Archimedean framework while still accounting for infinitesimal quantities - a choice previously formalised by Stewart. A further consequence of our confirmation of the infinitesimal method's compatibility with the fundamental principle of the exchange principle is that Arthur's initial argument against Leibniz's use of infinitesimal methods is no longer tenable. In response to claims by Arthur and Rabouin, our confirmation of the infinitesimal method's compatibility also renders obsolete their reasoning for supposing that Leibniz's concept of infinitesimals is inherently self-contradictory, a notion previously noted by early Knobloch. Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition. In addition, we examine an application of this result in the context of ordered groups. Last, we outline some unresolved questions and potential areas for further investigation.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods that integrate graph data for item ranking have gained prominence due to the critical role of graphs in various applications. Graph-based recommender systems primarily focus on exploiting item connections, despite user preferences also being influenced by interpersonal relationships. This research introduces a novel graph-based method that leverages user-item similarity graphs constructed with neural networks to optimize recommendations, surpassing existing benchmarks in performance. Furthermore, we propose a framework to create training data for these similarity graphs on a large scale by utilizing existing ratings. This framework enables the exploitation of numerous available ratings for rating prediction, thereby enhancing the bias-variance equilibrium. Experimental results on three real-world datasets show the significant superiority of our proposed algorithm over state-of-the-art recommender systems in terms of performance. Notably, our approach exhibits the best performance when used for explaining top-rated items. This is because our method is capable of learning user and item representations that are aggregated to predict ratings, thereby facilitating easier understanding of rated items. Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. Building upon this understanding, we derive an infinitesimal freeness expectation formula for any given polynomial expression involving random matrices, thereby enabling the calculation of expectation values of specific polynomials applied to these matrices. We also demonstrate the applicability of this approach to derive exact expectations for particular polynomial expressions over the entire spectrum of these matrices. As a concrete application, we use this formalism to derive exact expectations for specific polynomials applied to GOE matrices, thereby addressing a long-standing problem known as the Sixty-Fourth Problem in the field of random matrix theory. Notably, our approach offers a versatile method for deriving exact expectations for a broad class of polynomial expressions involving random matrices, which can be readily extended and applied to specific matrix ensembles such as GUE, GOE, etc. In doing so, we gain a unified perspective on various random matrix models. Furthermore, we confirm that the proposed infinitesimal freeness formula is capable of reproducing existing findings for specific matrix ensembles, while also yielding novel results.
