This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods that take advantage of 'good' or 'bad' time intervals to improve efficiency. These techniques are inspired by similar ideas in flow monitoring. For metric logic, we suggest creating a time interval automaton that helps to recognize 'good' system behaviors by mapping concrete time intervals to symbolic ones. This approach simplifies the complex automaton of metric ITL and reduces the recognition problem to a simpler state recognition problem. For Timed B\"uchi Automata, we develop a flow monitoring method that adapts online to adjust the time scale, allowing us to recognize 'good' system behaviors with linearly scaled time. This method involves monitoring the system with a modified, adjusted automaton that adapts to the current time scale. Both methods allow for the monitoring of real-time systems that satisfy properties expressed either in metric ITL or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. This adaptation comes with a price, however, as the adjusted automata may become larger. Despite this limitation, we show that, under certain conditions, our monitoring method can be more efficient than direct comparison with actual time values. Experimental evaluations also demonstrate the practical effectiveness of these techniques. Symbolically representing time intervals offers a flexible solution that can be applied to various time scales, making it particularly useful for monitoring systems that operate at different time scales. As such, we propose a new representation for time intervals, called 'etervals', which easily adapts to both linear and non-linear time scales. This representation, combined with the efficient monitoring methods we developed, provides a comprehensive solution for monitoring real-time systems. This combined effort allows for the efficient recognition of 'good' system behaviors over various time scales, either directly through the use of etervals or indirectly by simplifying complex automata. This research is based on prior work with flow monitoring and time scales, as well as efficient monitoring methods for MCTL. This new approach, however, offers a significant improvement in efficiency, even for difficult properties and large time scale adjustments. As such, it provides a suitable replacement for direct comparison with actual time values in real-time system monitoring. This new method also shares some similarities with related ideas in parameterized verification, where the system's parameters are adjusted to reduce the complexity of the recognition problem. Unlike these ideas, however, our approach focuses on adapting the time scale itself to improve the efficiency of recognizing 'good' system

Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a limited set of supplier doubling dimension values and a specified number of anomalies. Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center issue - a subset of CkSwO, - we demonstrate that achieving an analogous parameterized solution when dealing with highway dimension is computationally challenging, falling under the W[1] hardness class, whereas we find it relatively simpler with doubling dimension values. This distinction is the first documented case where a problem exhibits W[1] hardness with highway dimension, despite being manageable with doubling dimension values. Additionally, we apply three novel taxonomies to categorize centers in networks, leading to improved time complexity in solving the Capacitated $k$-Center issue for centers with limited neighbors (at most) three times as expensive as the cheapest option. This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, expand existing methods, and propose new ones. Notably, we demonstrate that all known methods fall into one of two categories, before introducing a landmark discovery - some of these methods can be optimized to yield more efficient results. Additionally, we tackle the problem of its own variant, involving error-prone polynomial system solving, providing not only a more efficient evaluation strategy but also a general-purpose algorithm for this particular problem. This work is complemented by a companion submission, which provides an in-depth analysis of our proposed methods, accompanied by a wealth of numerical demonstrations and code snippets on https://polysolve.github.io, serving as a resource for further exploration and potential improvements. This includes the implementation of our techniques in the existing Polysolve library. This is the second submission in an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors. The first submission appeared at ARXIV in 2019 under the title "Solving Polynomial Linear Systems with Errors: Part I." Both submissions are authorized by arXiv preprint series cs.CR arXIV:1904.04899.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is enhanced by the parity symmetry, primarily due to its impact on the reduced density matrix. The possibility of observing this parity-symmetry protected quenching of photon bundle emission depends on the ultrastrong coupling parameter $\lambda$. If $\lambda > \kappa/2$, the phenomenon becomes visible, resulting in a significant increase in the photon bundle's purity compared to a situation without parity symmetry. The discovery of protected quenching enables the exploration of parity-symmetry protected photon bundle emission, enabling the precise study of Rabi oscillations and cavity fields in the deep strong coupling regime. Furthermore, the findings of the study can be used to develop a parity-symmetry protected quantum processor utilizing the Rabi model. The processor would facilitate the protected observation of quenching in photon bundle emission, as well as the secure transfer of data between qubits within a parity-symmetry protected subspace. The data transfer would involve a series of parity-symmetry protected quantum gates, such as the parity-symmetry protected CNOT gate, which would enable the accurate manipulation of qubits and maintain parity-symmetry protected operations. The parity-symmetry protected quantum processor could be used to implement protected algorithms, while the parity-symmetry protected quenching of photon bundle emission could be used for the detection of parity-symmetry protected photon bundle emission. The detection would involve a comparison between the parity-symmetry protected and parity-symmetry broken situations, which would require adjusting the ultrastrong coupling parameter $\lambda$ to exceed half the dissipation rate $\kappa$. The parity-symmetry protected quantum processor and the parity-symmetry protected quenching of photon bundle emission are the key outcomes of the study, which makes the detection of photon bundle emission in the Rabi model a valuable resource for quantum science and technology. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. Additionally, the derived equation of state shows excellent agreement with experimental data and historical measurements in the subcritical domain of cesium, providing a valuable contribution to the field of fundamental gas dynamics and heat transfer. Furthermore, the study offers insights into critical properties, providing a realistic assessment of the critical point location for group IA elements, according to predictions derived from van der Waals scaling theories. Modeling the critical behavior of group IA elements according to scaling theories suggests the existence of a critical value for the gas-giant atom size and a critical temperature for the thermodynamic equilibrium of group IA elements, both of which are substantially higher than the experimentally measured critical temperatures of the group's individual members. Applying the principle of corresponding states to the group's behavior, these values are estimated to be approximately $3.85\cdot R$ and $3\cdot T_r$, respectively, where $R$ is the gas constant and $t_r$ is the reduced temperature scale factor. A semi-empirical equation for determining the speed of sound in alkali metals has also been obtained, as well as mathematical expressions for deriving key thermodynamic properties from the equation of state, thereby confirming the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. Our innovative approach involves the rapid dissemination and aggregation of unique node IDs within the network through the application of priority flood protocols, resulting in the creation of an intricate sparse subgraph with properties suitable for the estimation of its own size. Our algorithm extends the existing work in the field of distributed computing, specifically in the realm of sparse networks, and offers a valuable contribution. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. Our findings indicate that this method is a reliable alternative for determining metric variables in simulations with complex matter configurations. In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models, enabling these models to recognize dimensional connections and forecast outcomes for individual dimensions. Our framework, AD-Informer, has outperformed existing methods on multivariate forecasting tasks, according to experimental results. Notably, it has exhibited a notable balance between high accuracy and efficient inference times. As such, it is particularly suited to real-world applications where safety and efficiency are paramount. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors rely on either changing wavelength or changing distance. In our study, a novel approach utilizing a Littrow configuration is presented, offering a configuration that can correct dispersion by using a mirror and a single optical element, while maintaining a compact setup. Different designs can be selected based on various parameters including aperture size, field of view, and spectral range. To validate the proposed concept, a comprehensive analysis using adaptive optics simulations was performed, demonstrating its applicability and effectiveness. Specifically, this correction is anticipated to significantly improve infrared observations made off-axis. Various design options are presented, starting with a 60cm telescope specific model that achieved a correction of 0.3 arcseconds, matching telescope point spread function accuracy across a 1.2 micron wavelength range. Alternative designs are also provided for either reducing the system's overall length or incorporating an image rotator for additional applications. A detailed explanation of these optical design principles is presented in an accompanying paper. As a result, this Littrow-based ADC offers a compact, efficient solution, paving the way for innovative infrared astronomical observations and providing a viable option for existing telescopes. Additionally, this design may also be adapted for non-astronomical applications, such as laser communications or chemistry-based experiments. Furthermore, this concept can still be improved upon by utilizing materials with lower dispersion. By utilizing this Littrow configuration, this variant of ADC can provide a comprehensive combination of corrected imagery, rotational sensing, and compact setup, thereby making it a versatile tool across various scientific domains. Rare-earth doped glasses could also serve as an alternative option to achieve this correction. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address a distillation method that incorporates multiple knowledge sources - from a ranking model's fine-tuning and its pre-training - to magnify a target model's performance using its own knowledge. Our distillation method comprises two stages: initial training, where we acquire knowledge through the target model's pre-training; and subsequent fine-tuning, where we integrate knowledge from both the target model's pre-training and fine-tuning phases. Through theoretical analysis and experimental proof on the Clicks-51K dataset, we demonstrate that our method surpasses other ranking models and distillation techniques. Notably, our findings show that incorporating knowledge from both sources can boost performance by as much as 0.0374 in nDCG@10 when compared to excluding knowledge from fine-tuning. Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable through its impact on short-range quantum systems, particularly in experiments examining the near-zero-frequency component of dark matter-induced fluctuations in isolated particles or small groups of particles. A theoretical framework is developed for such a detection approach, with analytical calculations confirming that, according to standard models, this method should not yield detectable results. Additionally, the analysis includes simulations involving real-world data sets from the QUANTUMUNIT experiment involving up to three particles. Ultimately, the findings suggest that this detection approach is not currently capable of providing evidence for bosonic dark matter. However, the approach may be utilized to establish limits on bosonic dark matter models that differ from the generally accepted "ultralight" model. Future improvements to the experiment and its analysis may lead to a detectable signal. Furthermore, the theoretical framework could be applied to other experiments involving quantum systems and may find additional applications in the field of ultralight dark matter research. A companion arXiv posting includes detailed mathematical derivations, experiment simulations, and discussion of the results. This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established via a characterization framework. The characteristics of BPC's solution include being the mean of the convex hull of a system of linear equations and being the extremal point of that hull if it exists. The study shows that solutions are unique and sparse for a wide range of frequencies, up to approximately 2Kc. The BPC algorithm is further analyzed in terms of its optimality and existence, along with investigations into the optimality of sparse solutions. The paper also derives upper and lower bounds for the number of non-zero Fourier components of sparse solutions, yielding approximately 4Kc upper and 2Kc lower bounds. The BPC solution is demonstrated to be the minimum total variation among all sparse Radon measures through a convex decomposition approach. The paper ultimately establishes upper and lower bounds for the number of non-zero Fourier components in sparse solutions through the total variation analysis. The research finds that the upper and lower bounds converge to each other as Kc increases without limit, while the total variation decreases at a logarithmic rate and eventually approaches a constant value. The BPC solution is shown to converge in probability to a continuous measure with a finite total variation as Kc tends to infinity. The convergence is also observed in the L^p norm for any p in the range of 1 to 2. The research finds that the total variation is approximately logarithmically scaled in Kc, ultimately achieving a constant value. The BPC solution was previously known to be sparse, but the total variation was previously undetermined. A minimum total variation criterion is used to select the extremal point from the convex hull of a system of linear equations, thereby refining the previous total variation estimate. The research also establishes the continuity of the minimum total variation function through the continuity of its gradient, thereby bypassing Chincarini's and Ciarlet-Manchetti's results on the continuity of minimum distance functions. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have issues with numerical oscillations when solving the vector transport equation, which is particularly pronounced when higher-order elements are used in the solution variable. This limitation means that finite element methods based on the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements are not suitable for solving advection-diffusion problems, which are fundamental in a range of applications including fluid dynamics and bio-medical flow. This document describes a novel finite element method that mitigates these numerical oscillations by using the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements for the vector transport equation and a continuous-element approach to approximate the solution variable. Specifically, we leverage the continuous-element method introduced in [C. Bernard, J. Hue, and G. Pong, Journal of Computational Physics, vol. 404, 2022], which combines a higher-order element for the solution function with a lower-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas element for the fluxes. This continuous-element method eliminates numerical oscillations while maintaining stability, which enables the development of a convergent method for solving advection-diffusion problems. Furthermore, we provide error estimates that validate the method's convergence. Lastly, we present numerical results that demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy in solving such problems. This is accomplished by implementing the method in code and analyzing the resulting simulations. Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions, and (3) the ability to learn from abundant video data.
Comprising modules for attention, convolution, and pooling, HAN efficiently
extracts salient information from video data. Experimental evaluations on 
two benchmark datasets, TUECHNICAL and TARTAR, demonstrate superior performance 
for a range of human action classification tasks. Moreover, HAN offers a notable 
advantage over existing methods in capturing video temporal structures. As a 
result, HAN is well-suited for applications involving the visual understanding 
of human actions in motion. A related implementation can be found at https://github.com/huahtk/HAN.

Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Results show that Nested Sampling successfully calculates entropy and mutual information in all scenarios, comparing favorably to alternative methods. Furthermore, this approach also enables the estimation of parameters like hyperentropies that describe distribution characteristics. Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, especially with the rise of digital technologies that rely on the internet. The consequences of a single cybersecurity breach can be severe, giving small businesses an added incentive to prioritize internet and network security. This study aims to examine the current cybersecurity measures among small businesses in Bulacan, Philippines. By distributing questionnaires to 50 owners or key personnel of various small businesses in the region, we gathered data on their awareness of cybersecurity threats and existing security protocols. Our results indicate a disconnect between the perceived importance of cybersecurity and the actual implementation of security measures. Consequently, we recommend that awareness campaigns be directed towards educating owners and key personnel about the significance of cybersecurity. Additionally, initiatives should be undertaken to provide them with accessible and affordable cybersecurity solutions. Our findings may serve as reference points for other similar studies in the future. This study was made possible by a grant from the Philippine Council for Research and Development (DOST-PCRD).

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancy that inevitably arises from various theoretical assumptions inherent in all measurement activities. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be addressed by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It is found that the commonly adopted statistical techniques not only generate non-universal equations but also assume that the law's evolution dimensions are known beforehand, a problem addressed by using multi-faceted ensemble learning methods that can automatically detect the law's dimensions and accurately predict the trajectories with minimal data required. However, it is discovered that the resulting equations, though dimensionally correct, are only approximate due to inherent uncertainties inherent in all measurement activities. Ultimately, this means that the formulation of a universal physical law from measurement data must be considered a futile endeavor, and all measurement activities must be grounded in and informed by a set of well-established and fundamental physical principles. This understanding leads to the development of novel data-driven methods of automated physics discovery, such as "physics-informed neural network" and "physics-emergent neural network," both of which are grounded in and informed by a set of well-established and fundamental physical principles. These methods not only accurately predict the trajectories with minimal data required but also identify the theoretical-measurement discrepancy that arises from various theoretical assumptions inherent in all measurement activities, thereby confirming the fundamental principles of mechanics through numerical experiments. This confirms that these methods offer a more practical and efficient approach to resolving long-standing issues in physics and could potentially be used for inferring unknown physical principles and governing equations in various fields of engineering and astrophysics. Furthermore, this ground-breaking research demonstrates the need for a more profound understanding of the interplay between AI, ML, data, and reality, and it seeks to answer it through a set of fundamental questions. Ultimately, this is aimed at inspiring a new wave of research in the fields of AI, ML, and physics, and it is hoped that this will lead to the creation of computevergent, collaborative, and inclusive environments that foster the innovation of novel AI, ML, and physics techniques. This is aimed at addressing many more pressing issues in various fields of engineering and astrophysics, such as predicting complex astrophysical phenomena and space missions.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that allows researchers to explore the vibrational modes of amorphous materials around their boson peak frequency. Neutrons interact with the material's atoms via a short-range, central force, which enables direct measurement of the vibrational density of states. This is contrasted with the longitudinal and transverse acoustic modes, which are typically difficult to observe directly with inelastic scattering but can be inferred through Brillouin scattering, a higher-frequency, wave-vector-limited measurement of the material's elasticity. Neutron inelastic scattering can typically access a limited section of the material's density of states, often including the boson peak and surrounding regions. The interaction of neutrons with various modes of vibration in atoms allows for a direct measurement of the material's vibrational density of states, and comparing this with the sum of modes obtained through density functional theory provides a measure of the material's dynamic structure factor. This difference indicates how much the material's elasticity is affected by its disorder at a given frequency, and such studies have been conducted on a range of glasses. This research finds the difference to be quite small in some cases, on the order of 10 percent, but significantly higher, at around 50 percent, for other glasses. Further investigation into this phenomenon will help clarify the relationship between the material's structure, its boson peak, and its elastic properties. This thesis presents the results of neutron inelastic scattering measurements of several glass-forming materials, examining their vibrational density of states and comparing it with the mode counts obtained through density functional theory. Additionally, the materials studied include three silicon-based glasses, a boron-silicon glass, and a tungsten-titanium amorphous alloy. The findings of this research show that the mode and neutron data agree well for most of the measured frequency range but differ at higher frequencies at about 45 percent for two of the silicon-based glasses and a boron-silicon glass, and at about 30 percent for a third silicon-based glass and the tungsten-titanium alloy. The frequency at which these differences occur corresponds to the material's boson peak frequency, and such differences have not been observed in a rare-earth-based glass-boron. Further study is needed to clarify the connection between the material's structure, its boson peak, and its elastic properties. This thesis presents the results of neutron inelastic scattering measurements of several glass-forming materials, examining their vibrational density of states and comparing it with the mode counts obtained through density functional theory.

This sequential framework exhibits a striking balance of diversity and quality in the obtained solutions. To evaluate the performance of these integrated approaches, we utilize a suite of benchmark problems as well as a real-world benchmark from the fields of biology and medicine. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with its environment, embedded in a code-specific game environment where winning strategies translate to efficient decoding techniques. Through this environmental approach, the paper introduces policies to tackle the conventional problems of syndrome extraction, Bell-test implementation, and general full fault-tolerant decoding, and further utilizing policy-based decoding proves capable of handling multiple types of common errors during quantum computation. Experimental validations of these methods were conducted using small surface codes for the Pauli $X$ and $Z$ errors. This contribution offers a novel approach to topological decoding, introducing an alternative perspective that might be more easily extensible to complex scenarios than traditional belief propagation methods. Additionally, it highlights the potential for continuing research in environmental decoding by demonstrating its application to realistic, albeit slightly larger codes. This adds to previous studies that employed decoding using neural networks in quantum error correction. Notably, the breakthrough involved developing a winning strategy for the full fault-tolerant decoding challenge with a 8-qubit surface code for the first time. This achievement is preceded by successful implementations of policy-based decoding for 5- and 6-qubit surface codes. Experiments using a quantum simulator verified the efficacy of the developed winning strategies in realistic scenarios, validating the environmental approach as a viable means of solving topological decoding problems, and showing that neural networks can approximate winning strategies more efficiently than traditional back-propagation methods. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results show that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations. Moreover, the inherent errors in this approach can be mitigated through a phase-encoding technique without increasing the number of required gates. Our findings also suggest that as the precision of gate operations increases, the effects of connectivity and coherence decay become more pronounced, highlighting the importance of considering these factors even with high precision. Using a scaling analysis, our work addresses the broad question of how the characteristics of digital-analog quantum computers change as the precision approaches the Planck scale. Furthermore, our research delimits the parameter regime in which digital-analog computing can effectively simulate physical systems, suggesting that a much larger number of operations may be required to reach this limit. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, representing an ideal scenario where the model is both accurate and robust. 

By starting with this feature set, our method enables the model to converge towards this benchmark, represented by an $\epsilon-approximate$ set of tasks, where it can confidently predict on $\epsilon$-similar tasks. 

In our experiments, this approach surpasses state-of-the-art robustness methods in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios, even under adversarial conditions. 

Notably, this method is particularly effective when combined with task clustering, where similar tasks are grouped together to reduce the model's optimization target. 

As a result, the model can achieve significantly better performance on OoD scenarios, amounting to as much as a 20.95% improvement in robust accuracy and a 9.07% improvement in robustness-agnostic accuracy when compared to the state-of-the-art. 

You can view our code here: https://github.com/zwang84/Simple-Robust-OoD. 

Additionally, you can find our benchmarked results here: https://robustbench.org/. 

It's worth noting that our approach shares a common goal with robustness-agnostic methods: achieving high accuracy on a task and generalizing well to similar tasks, where possible, or to novel environments, where predicted distributions serve as a guide. 

As such, we've modified some of these methods to behave more like robustness-agnostic approaches, rather than robustness-sensitive ones, by removing dependency on OoD data and cross-task similarity metrics. 

We've found that our approach consistently surpasses these methods in task-specific and cross-task accuracy, as validated by repeated experiments. 

You can find the modified code here: https://github.com/zwang84/Simple-Robust-OoD. 

We've conducted our experiments on CIFAR10 and ImageNet, employing both robustness-agnostic and robustness-sensitive methods, where available, and leveraging the RoboBench benchmark to ensure fairness and reproducibility.

To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes binary-driven micro-mechanisms and a localized speech actuation method, minimizing system artifacts and facilitating the generation of intricate 3D structures. Our joint approach has successfully created various computational algorithms and contributed to the advancement of dynamic wavefront manipulation in optical devices. Our findings have far-reaching applications in speech processing, optical communication, and biomedical imaging, among other fields. Examples of our results include the construction of a 51-element binary mask, used to form a 3D cube with an optical efficiency of 92.6%, and the creation of 55 intricate structures with an average optical efficiency of 84.4% across diverse scattering environments. These breakthroughs demonstrate our algorithm's capability to overcome light scattering noise and achieve unprecedented levels of precision and optical efficiency in forming complex structures within and through disordered mediums. Our work has broad applications in computational algorithms, speech processing, optical communication, and biomedical imaging. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can accurately synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators employ a bias-reducing approach, namely the bias correction of Liang and Zeger, and the bias correction of Mullahy.  Both estimators have been implemented in R and tested through simulation based on a variant of the Fleischman data.  Results have shown that the newly developed estimators perform well even in cases of a limited number of studies and correctly control for Type 1 errors.  Both estimators have been added to the userfriendly R package'meta', with implementations of various cluster-robust estimators and a convenient function to facilitate user selection of the most appropriate estimator.  A practical approach is suggested for determining the most suitable estimator based on a selected threshold of acceptable bias and the difference in variances between results obtained through the use of robust estimators and those derived from traditional pairwise meta-analyses.  Guidance is provided on how to choose the specified threshold, with alternative criteria suggested for this decision. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. This method surpasses existing approaches in our knowledge domain by grouping related sub-networks and assigning topic densities in addition to probabilities. Furthermore, our model facilitates the creation of customizable, multi-level categorizations and dynamic, adaptive schemas tailoring the depth of each hierarchy to the underlying data. Ultimately, our empirical findings demonstrate that HDTM's robust performance and efficiency make it an excellent choice for large-scale Internet applications. As such, we've developed a flexible open-source implementation incorporating Spark for distributed processing, as well as a comprehensive dataset called Wikipedia_2012 comprising 754 million words and 7 million documents, available for public download. This implementation, along with the implementation details and demo code, can be found at https://csci5588.github.io/. Additional resources are provided in Section 7. logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, we define a subobject classifier in this simplified hyperdoctrine and demonstrate the representation of predicates within it. 
Finally, we select a metric space within the category and define subobjects relative to it, incorporating these notions into a hyperdoctrine framework. 
This hyperdoctrine can be compared to that of Siani-McKey, Ramsey-Majer, and Löb, providing an alternative perspective. 
Specifically, we observe that the second inverse of the subobject classifier in our hyperdoctrine corresponds to the maximal consistent set in Siani-McKey's arrangement. 
Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between the universal property of the subobject classifier in our hyperdoctrine and that of Löb's. 
Consequently, we are able to formulate Löb's principle in the context of the hyperdoctrine, and prove that it can be reduced to a version of the Boolean closed complementation axiom. 
Similarly, we apply the same method to derive a hyperdoctrine framework for extended continuous logic and examine corresponding versions of the axioms for infinitary fixed-point logic. 
Ultimately, we conclude with the observation that the choice of metric space in our arrangement is inherently arbitrary. 
Consequently, any consistent extension of the theory must encompass a consistent assignment of predicates to any chosen metric space. 
This property suggests the need for a more flexible approach to proof theory, one that can accommodate proof systems grounded in metric spaces rather than being tied to specific syntactic schemes.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-frequency observations of Ecological Momentary Assessment data and synchronized, sporadic readings of Electronic Health Records. Our models leverage Ecological Momentary Assessment data, alongside Electronic Health Records, to make predictions. Notably, incorporating Ecological Momentary Assessment data improves the accuracy of predictions over relying solely on Electronic Health Records. Furthermore, the proposed method surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art methods, including deep sequential models, in a dataset simulation environment. In addition, the inherent complexity of forecasting suicidal ideation, particularly from Electronic Health Records, is mitigated by leveraging the collective information provided by both data sources. In terms of feature selection, most value lies in clinical variables like depression scores and medication usage, with the relative importance of variables being dynamic and predictive-target dependent. Thorough experiments were conducted to validate the method's effectiveness across diverse suicidal ideation prediction tasks. In practical applications, the method can be employed to anticipate and support at-risk individuals, informing targeted interventions. As such, the method holds substantial moral and ethical implications for enhancing our understanding of suicidal behavior and directing life-saving interventions. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies are found across a wide range of stellar masses, while S galaxies are more prevalent in the lower-mass spectrum. In contrast, U galaxies are relatively rare in the high-mass regime. Using the STARDUST model, we determined that U galaxies are approximately 1.3 times more effective at producing far-ultraviolet light than S galaxies of similar mass. Our analysis further indicates that U galaxies are likely surrounded by a gas disk that is partially collapsed or has a highly irregular shape. We investigated various mechanisms that could cause warping in these galaxies, including the presence of a massive dark matter halo and an active galactic nucleus. Our findings suggest that U galaxies are characterized by elevated gas turbulence and a flattened distribution of dark matter, which may contribute to warping. Additionally, U galaxies show signs of gas depletion due to star formation, prompting the need for more detailed studies of U galaxies with higher resolution and accuracy. Our research paves the way for further investigation into the properties and evolution of U galaxies. The automatic identification and quantification of road damage is crucial for assessing the condition of roads, which is essential for predicting maintenance needs and allocating budget. While research has made significant progress in achieving these goals, implementing these advancements in real-world settings can be challenging, especially for municipalities with limited resources. To address these difficulties, this study examined solutions that allow municipalities to leverage existing staff as data collectors to identify road conditions efficiently. Two key approaches were explored: one where staff collects data manually, and another where staff collects data through images, which are then analyzed using machine learning to predict road conditions. Our findings indicate that both methods are effective, although the image-based approach is more efficient. Furthermore, combining human and machine-based methods reveals that they complement each other well, suggesting that these strategies can be used in conjunction with other technologies to optimize road condition assessment. Ultimately, the choice of strategy depends on the municipality's specific requirements and the capabilities of its staff. If staff members can accurately identify road conditions through data collection without needing additional support, the manual method may be the better choice. However, if staff require training to collect image data, the efficiency gains make this an attractive option. Additionally, analyzing data collected through images can also detect other issues not initially searched for, which further enhances its effectiveness. Conversely, manual data collection means these resources are exclusively devoted to data collection, with no image processing requirements. By understanding these trade-offs, municipalities can choose the approach that best utilizes their existing staff, allowing them to incorporate automated road damage evaluation into their maintenance practices more effectively. At present, municipalities with limited resources are best suited by the image-based model, which has shown superior efficiency. Notably, our study's findings are an expansion on earlier work, which had established that this approach was possible but was explored further here. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in transferring the expert's actions to similar scenarios, particularly when the environments are dissimilar from each other and from the expert's domain.  Current state-of-the-art systems fall short when faced with tasks that require long-term planning to achieve goals in new, unfamiliar environments.  In this study, a new imitation learning system is proposed that leverages the power of model checking to ensure the accuracy of imitation learning.  It does this by assuming the model can represent both the expert and agent states, allowing the agent to verify its actions against the expert's through a formal verification process.  The model is represented using the $\mathcal{MVL}$ language, allowing the agent to generate and verify actions that achieve specific goals in new, unfamiliar environments.  The effectiveness of the proposed system was tested on two benchmark domains - the kitchen and the mobile manipulation domain.  Results show it outperforms existing imitation learning methods while achieving comparable performance to model-based reinforcement learning.  The work includes a theoretical evaluation but finds that the current verification approach becomes computationally infeasible as the state space grows larger.  Alternative approaches to addressing this issue are suggested.  The source code for the model and experiments can be accessed at: https://github.com/achittala/MVL-IQL. Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications of the form "if a set of items A occurs, then a target item B also occurs" which are expressed as A -> B. We focus on extending classic concepts of confidence and support to generalize partial implications. Our approach distinguishes between occurrences of items, transactions, and their frequencies. We aims to explore the lattice structure of all possible partial implications and their associated frequencies. Our method requires solving a linear equation and incurring costs that are at most quadratic with respect to the number of items. We then derive spectral generalizations of partial implications by applying Principal Component Analysis. We focus on two types of occurrences: itemsets and individual items. Our approach involves computing the top itemsets and their frequencies. We show that the costs of computing spectral generalizations are at most linear with respect to the number of items. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Specific to our data, every dollar spent on treatment beyond initial costs would be compensated by $1.40 to $1.60 in crime prevention.  A subsequent look at how receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence affects an offender's chances of being re-incarcerated within a three-year time frame reveals a 23 percent or 3.6 percentage points decrease in those chances.  Receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowers an offender's chances of being incarcerated following a new conviction by 35 percent or 5.8 percentage points.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future incarceration costs could more than cover the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Specific to our data, every dollar spent on treatment beyond initial costs would be compensated by $2 to $2.50 in crime prevention.  A possible explanation for these findings could be that mental health treatment as part of their sentence allows offenders to plead guilty to lesser charges, though this hypothesis requires further investigation.  Another potential explanation could be that mental health treatment as part of their sentence reduces future offending by altering the offender's behavior while they are on probation, though this hypothesis also requires further investigation.  A possible path for further research in determining the effectiveness of mental health treatment as part of their sentence would be to examine data that records an offender's contacts with crime victims, cites, charges, and disposition.  Ultimately the ultimate goal of this research is to facilitate a thorough cost-benefit analysis of different sentencing options that could guide judges in making more informed decisions in sentencing hearings.  This research also could potentially spur policy changes at a state level that encourage judges to sentence offenders

This paper outlines AnSOR, a system designed to identify unusual patterns in discrete time series data by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. AnSOR operates within a real-time framework, generating compact representations of individual time series episodes using Hidden Markov Models, and then employs clustering algorithms to detect and highlight data anomalies. To validate its effectiveness, AnSOR was tested on three distinct datasets, comparing its performance against existing anomaly detection methods. Notably, AnSOR outperformed existing approaches on the SEAME dataset and demonstrated comparable results on the power consumption dataset from the University of California, Berkeley. Furthermore, AnSOR successfully identified a vehicle collision incident in the Uber dataset. Overall, AnSOR's capabilities prove valuable in extracting meaningful insights from time series data while minimizing resource requirements. Its implementation is openly available online.

It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. These estimators offer improved performance over the estimators from LaMont and Zinziar (2017), with the estimators being more flexible and generalised by incorporating the GMLE's consistent estimations that are easily computed. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, an algorithm based on postprocessing random sampling is proposed, along with an evaluation of its efficacy through mathematical analysis. Lastly, an empirical study is conducted to compare the performance of this new approach with existing methods. As a result, significant improvements can be achieved by taking into account the dependencies between records, leading to higher data utility with the same level of privacy protection. Additionally, the proposed postprocessing random sampling method outperforms a renowned differential privacy framework, known for its efficiency in handling record dependencies. These findings validate the one-sided differential privacy framework, demonstrating its capability to handle complex dependencies between data records effectively. In particular, it offers superior data utility to traditional approaches, making it a more suitable choice for applications with dependent records. In terms of implementation, an open-source toolkit, known as OSDF, is utilized to verify the efficacy of the proposed framework, showcasing its practicality and usability in real-world scenarios. In protoplanetary disks, it is not uncommon to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and pre-existing constraints from data analysis and radiative transfer calculations.
By analyzing our model results, we discovered that they mirror the observed gas substructures and provide insights into the distribution of gas within the disk.
The best-fitting model reveals a distinct gas surface density pattern with two distinct parts, each with a different decrease rate as you move further out.
This unique pattern, combined with existing metal-to-radius ratios from previous studies, enable accurate predictions of various species' abundance distributions.
The model also indicates that C and O are equally abundant when considering their relative abundances by mass.
Furthermore, our model suggests two possible explanations that may lead to the observed gas substructures, the first being the effects of a planet with a distance of approximately 13 abuits, and the second being a fragment of a large planetesimal with a distance of approximately 30 abuits. Both of these scenarios show promising matches to observations. 
The model also indicates that gas turbulence may have a significant impact on the distribution of different species' abundances. 
In order to confirm our findings, we suggest future observations utilizing high angular resolution spectroscopy with facilities like VLT/GRACES or LMT. 
In addition, we suggest that future findings in AS 209 should be compared with existing data on another system with similar properties to further understand the physics governing gas substructures.

Our long-term goal is to establish ETA as an official, stand-alone application that serves the needs of particle physics research, and we welcome contributions from the scientific community to further develop and expand our tool. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated. As an additional byproduct of this work, we establish the short-time uniqueness of solutions to a specific first-order mean field game of controls with a similar regularity constraint applied to dependence of the Lagrangian function on positions, and also demonstrate the closeness of the short-time unique solution to the corresponding limiting measure, which is itself solution to the mean field game of controls. Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing specifically on their spatial patterns, movement within the galaxy, and potential origins. By examining the distribution of these structures in relation to nearby star clusters, we found that these structures are not physically connected entities but rather dispersing groups, separated from each other by large distances. Furthermore, our spatial analysis revealed an uneven pattern in the distribution of these structures across the galaxy, suggesting that they are linked to larger dynamical movements, specifically the galactic spiral arm's rotational pattern. Additionally, we discovered that these structures tend to move at a varying rate, with some moving faster than expected and others moving slower, contradicting the idea that these groups are gravitationally bound systems. Based on these findings, we propose an alternative explanation, that these structures originated from the disruption of star clusters by the galactic tidal force, resulting in loosely connected groups, similar to those observed in the Ursa Major moving group. We also identified key indicators that these structures are not physically connected groups, but rather isolated groups, dispersed in the galaxy, providing potential criteria for classification and further analysis of these structures in the future. Ultimately, these newly discovered groups offer a unique insight into the breakdown of star clusters due to tidal disruption, expanding our understanding of these structures and their role in the galaxy's dynamics. This research has implications for how these structures are currently classified and studied, presenting new opportunities for further investigation and analysis. We provide readers with various visualization tools, including planetary maps, demonstrating the movement and distribution of these structures, based on the Gaia data set, available through the N.A.P.D. database. A special recognition is given to the Gaia collaboration for their outstanding work in developing the gaia data set, without which these discoveries would not be possible. Additionally, this research is supported by the Russian Federation's National Science Foundation, through grant 19-07-1000000. A complete list of participants is provided, at the end of this document. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual Incompatibility Metric (VIM), which adapts the concept of Remez polynomial approximation to calculate compatibility percentages for disjoint garment sets. By fine-tuning VIM using fashion expertise, we've discovered it can predict compatibility with high accuracy, outperforming existing classification-based approaches. Furthermore, VIM has the added benefit of enabling the creation of exclusive fashion items by quantizing VIM values, thus bridging the gap between visual aesthetics and computational models. To support our proposed method, we've developed an extensive 80K dataset called VIMedia, comprised of fashion items and their semantic attributes, along with labeled pairs of garments sets harvested from online fashion forums. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study makes two key contributions. Firstly, it proposes FedBuffGA, a FedBuff adaptation that incorporates the evolutionary algorithm, which optimizes model parameters by leveraging distributed fitness function evaluations. Secondly, the study conducts comprehensive empirical evaluations of FedBuffGA and existing solutions through challenging scenarios, including convex and convex-meshed non-convex objectives, across various network delay conditions. Results show that FedBuffGA consistently outperforms competitors, with performance enhancements ranging from 24% to 69%, depending on the scenario. Moreover, experiments validate the fairness, fairness-performance tradeoff, and fairness-fairness tradeoff properties of FedBuffGA. The associated code is available on GitHub at the provided URL.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators. Additionally, we identify a condition ensuring the commutant of the infinitesimal second shift semigroup is dense within the space of compact symmetric polynomial tempered distributions. Finally, we extend our findings to a real line convolution algebra associated with the Gaussian semigroup, demonstrating the identity of its functionals with a specific class of Bessel-type tempered distributions. Our methods draw heavily from previous work by Thangalsoy et al. and the functional calculus of Riesz-Marcinkiewicz, while also leveraging properties of special functions and the gamma product. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a novel connection between the gamma product and the Feynman integral, specifically in the context of the double wiener polynomial phase space. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether epitaxial matching to indium nitride or aluminum nitride can provide a solution. By combining first-principles calculations and semi-classical modeling, we found that while matching to indium nitride generates significant and desirable effects on the electron structure, it also worsens the hole mobility by increasing the hole effective mass. Conversely, matching to aluminum nitride yields opposite outcomes, with the hole mobility improving due to a decrease in the hole effective mass. However, it is the strain effects that provide the most promising results for gallium nitride when matched to aluminum nitride. A moderate uniaxial compressive strain causes the heavy holes to split into light and heavy holes, similar to what is observed in silicon. This change enhances the hole mobility by almost five times and makes gallium nitride compatible with a silicon-based platform. This finding holds potential for the seamless integration of gallium nitride and silicon power electronics. Our calculated results also show that the hole mobility in gallium nitride is most influenced by the piezoelectric strain generated by the aluminum nitride, with the electric field having a second-order effect. Finally, our work suggests that the piezoelectric strain has a more significant impact on the performance of gallium nitride than its mismatched thermal expansion. In conclusion, matching gallium nitride to aluminum nitride offers an attractive avenue for gallium nitride implementation in silicon power electronics. The successful application of our theoretical predictions relies on the achievement of a compressive uniaxial strain of around 8 kV/mm, which can be challenging in thin epitaxial layers. Nevertheless, recent advancements in growing ultra-smooth aluminum nitride templates provide an exciting prospect for the realization of strain engineering in gallium nitride and make our findings highly relevant to this field. In the long term, the concepts presented in this work have the potential to contribute to the development of efficient gallium nitride transistors, capable of handling over 1 MV/cm breakdown voltage and offering reduced on-resistance and fast switching speeds. This, in turn, paves the way for gallium nitride as a viable option for high-voltage and high-performance power electronics. In conclusion, the successful integration of gallium nitride with a silicon platform is essential for its implementation in power electronics. This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide a formula reminiscent of the Dobinski-like formula. To validate our findings, we compute the $\lambda$-analogues of known results involving Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. Our work is documented in a collection of papers and will be made available on arXiv in the coming weeks. In the first paper, we examine the $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials; in the second paper, we investigate the $\lambda$-analogues of reverse Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind; in the third paper, we explore the $\lambda$-analogues of strong Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind; in the fourth paper, we will delve into the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind as defined by Josefsson and in the final paper, we will examine the $\lambda$-analogues of rectilinear $\mathfrak{r}$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. Honored to be the first author, I, Kim, look forward to sharing our findings with the world.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings. Our findings indicate that SpliMe outperforms existing temporal KGE methods, and in addition, we identify issues with how static model performance on temporal data is typically evaluated, and provide two solutions to address these problems. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/alecgoodman/SpliMe.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements when combined. To facilitate future prompt development, we have made the prompt standard available on GitHub. The repository includes prompt examples, accompanying code, and an inventory of tasks and models examined in this study. It can be accessed at https://github.com/allamprods/what-do-prompts-look-like. As a result, we have developed the PROMPT taxonomy, which defines attributes common to all prompts and quantifies their variability. susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies highlights that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, and it's likely fueled by a small, low-mass star-forming cloud. Conversely, the HII region in the galaxy NGC 4605, which shares similar properties with UGC 8839, is significantly brighter and has a more exceptional location. Photospheric light from the HII region's star can be observed through a specialized, 0.8-micrometer bandpass, and it's suggested that this star has a significant chance of being exoplanet-habitable despite its high velocity and complex motion. Data from the GALEV project includes images of UGC 8839 at multiple wavelengths, including an observation of its near-infrared light, which can provide essential information for the study of rare, extreme star formations in galaxies. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, allowing them to act as photon sources. In the case of photon-hadron collisions, the photon source is the nucleus itself, and these collisions occur when these photons are seen as being 'virtually' exchanged between the nucleus and the incoming proton. This process is known as Ultra-Peripheral Collisions and is particularly prevalent in high-energy proton-nucleus interactions. In experiments, events resulting from these collisions can be re-created computationally using Monte-Carlo methods and are characterized by the transmission of the proton or nucleus with reduced energy, along with newly produced particles in the forward direction. Recent studies have shown the potential for exploring QED in the non-relativistic regime, and connections between photon-hadron collisions and photon-photon collisions are also being explored. This discussion will focus on the achievements and possibilities of exploring the data collected during the LHC Run 1, and we will highlight the specific findings related to lead-proton and uranium-proton collisions. Furthermore, we will discuss how future proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC may offer unique insights into the interactions of these particles. Ultimately, the goals of these studies are to contribute to a deeper understanding of the properties and behaviour of sub-nuclear matter and to uncover new phenomena that could lead to discoveries of significant significance. This discussion will provide an in-depth look at the latest research and future prospects in the field of photon-hadron collisions. Additionally, the contributions and implications of these collisions in the context of nuclear and particle physics will be extensively covered. This discussion is expected to provide a comprehensive overview of the latest developments and future directions in the field of photon-hadron collisions. In the concluding sections, we will examine how the research in this field may evolve in the near future and what new opportunities for exploration are anticipated to arise from both the completion of Phase 2 of the LHC project and the upcoming EIC and EPIC experiments. In the final part of this discussion, the achievements of the past and the prospects of the future will be summarized in order to provide a clear and concise overview of the developments and expectations in the field of photon-hadron collisions. This is especially relevant since these collisions represent an important area of research in the field of nuclear and particle physics and the upcoming experiments are anticipated

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline known as a counterfactual pipeline. The system's novel contribution lies in its ability to intervene in training data through the removal of specific examples, thereby enabling the computation of a conditional Shapley value. The system's performance has been rigorously evaluated through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, which demonstrate its practicality and usability in a real-world setting. The experiments specifically demonstrate the system's compatibility with counterfactual pipelines on various datasets, including a study of 62 potential interventions in a pipeline for predicting the price of housing. The system's name, DataScope, reflects its core functionality: it serves as a tool for intervening in training data to explain model behavior. The system's implementation is comprised of an intuitive command-line interface and a modular design that facilitates the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of counterfactual pipelines. The system's source code is freely accessible on GitHub under the terms of the Apache 2.0 open-source license.
