Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in under-determined inverse problems, such as generating images from limited data.  We examine this prior in the context of MRI, specifically a compressed sensing problem where we attempt to reconstruct an MRI image from sparse measurements taken at different orientations.  We can represent the generative prior as a learned function that maps measurements to a latent space, then combine this with an optimization approach that incorporates two main terms: a data fidelity term that ensures reconstructed images match the measurements, and a regularizer that enforces smoothness of the image, as well as a prior term that uses a generative model to predict the image based on measurements.  We can then formulate this as a non-convex problem and examine both inclusive and exclusive versions of the prior, as well as the impact of noise on the problem.  Our results show that using a generative prior outperforms a homoscedastic prior, and that incorporating the prior terms leads to a significant reconstruction improvement, especially in noisy conditions.  We also vary the amount of noise and measurements to examine their effects.  Our code is available online at the address: https://github.com/jeremybehling/compressed-sensing-gan.  Future research could involve incorporating physical information about the imaging process into the generative model.  Ultimately, our goal is to obtain high-resolution MRI images in low-cost, non-standard imaging scenarios.  Such applications may include lo-fi MRI scanners, quantitative MRI, eye MRI, MRI with non-standard orientations, MRI from few shots, MRI with sparse receiver coils, MRI from sparse time points.  In order to achieve this, our strategy is to combine iterative methods with deep learning-based approaches for solving inverse problems in MRI.  Specifically, we will examine and integrate various techniques for solving compressed sensing problems in MRI.  Our ultimate objective is to apply our method to DREAM MRI, a novel high-resolution MRI technique that uses multiple coils for data collection.  DREAM MRI outperforms traditional MRI by providing higher-resolution images in challenging, non-standard imaging scenarios.  To achieve this, our strategy is to combine several techniques for solving inverse problems in MRI, as well as comprehensive evaluation of our method to assess its performance. A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative QAOA parameter tuning methods like REBO or gradient-based approaches.  Our experiments with the exact problem solver, replaced by a Bayesian simulator due to the circuit's too-large a variation space for practical sampling, indicate that this quantum-classical approach yields desirable results. Moreover, our method shows promise in future applications where the circuit's parameters can be accurately modeled through probabilistic distributions, potentially outperforming other QAOA parameter tuning methods we've examined.  Even with our current limitations of being able to explore a finite portion of the variation space, our approach still achieves reasonable outcomes.  Future advancements in our tools may allow us to optimize this variant further.  In addition to its potential as a QAOA tuning method, our approach has applications in its own right, facilitating the use of quantum circuits for making Bayesian inferences within quantum computing environments.  This research is even more relevant given the ongoing development of quantum workloads that can be run on current hardware, as evidenced by projects like IBM's Quantum Experience that allow for simulation of quantum circuits with 53 qubits. A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area of two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant ellipse sectors and the additional triangles are combined using a weighted manner. The general form of the area calculation is provided along with a version specifically designed for nearly overlapping ellipses, where the secant lines are assumed to pass through the ellipse centers. The proposed algorithm is shown to be accurate, as demonstrated through numerous examples. Furthermore, it is also applied to determine the overlap area of an ellipse and a circle. The proposed method is adaptable to various applications in which the overlap area of different geometric shapes needs to be determined. It can be potentially extended to calculate the overlap areas of more intricate three-dimensional objects. The proposed approach is expected to benefit a wide range of applications in science and engineering. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the highest identification rate of 97.4% and surpassed the best comparable approach, which reported an identification rate of 94.7%, by significantly reducing the relative error rate. The proposed method's superiority is attributed to its ability to leverage anatomical knowledge of the spine, thus enabling the model to make more informed decisions in the presence of pathological variations. As a result, this approach offers a powerful tool for accurate vertebrae localization and identification in clinical contexts characterized by significant spinal pathologies. This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working independently and relying on their learned experiences - including critical decision-making - to guide their problem-solving processes.  Ultimately, these intelligent assistants become highly skilled software developers with the ability to design and implement robust, high-performance systems - a level of expertise that their expert counterparts may not have achieved.  The course then applies this concept to broader applications - such as medicine, education, and law - to create a new, intelligent workforce that systemically augments human capabilities and fuels a continuous cycle of improvement and growth in these fields.
